utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Will the registrar please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-95-14/2-R77-T, the Prosecutor versus Josip Jovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. David Ackerson on behalf of the Prosecution. I'm here with Salvatore Cannate, and Sebastiaan van Hooydonk, our case manager. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And for the accused?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I'm Kresimir Krsnik, attorney-at-law from Zagreb. I'm joined today by my legal assistant, Ms. Koraljka Tomasic, a member of the Croatian bar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ackerson, you are to present your case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may make a short opening, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: I would like to make a very brief opening, Your Honour. I would like to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may or if you think this is an appropriate time, my client would like to address the Chamber. My client would like to tell you a couple of words, by your leave, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is it about?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was precisely to explain, if you believe that to be necessary, why he failed to appear the last time around and to explain the reasons. We believe that it would be becoming to explain the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's not a fact in the case anymore. He's here. Let us proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: I just wanted to alert the AV booth that I'll be showing some Sanction slides during this presentation, and just to remind everyone that the protections on the witness in the case have been lifted, so I am going to refer to him by name, Stjepan Mesic. Your Honours, this is one of the simpler contempt cases you will encounter and at the same time it's one of the egregious of these newspaper contempt ones. The essential facts of this case revolve around the Croatian newspaper Slobodna Dalmacija. Slobodna Dalmacija was and it remains today one of the leading Croatian daily newspapers with a large circulation. It was readily available at all news-stands throughout Croatia in the year 2000. On December 1, 2000, Trial Chamber I served a cease and desist order on Slobodna Dalmacija, and there should be a slide showing on your screens right now. If it's not visible, please let me know. Is the slide visible to all the Chambers [sic]? Thank you. This court order demanded that Slobodna Dalmacija stop publishing the statements or closed session testimony of Stjepan Mesic who was a protected witness in the Blaskic case or be subject to charges of contempt. Slobodna Dalmacija chose to defy that order. Indeed, Slobodna Dalmacija published its intent to disobey the order on its front pages. It published the order itself and it then published the entirety of Mesic's closed session testimony across 22 issues in a brazen violation of the court order and in utter and open contempt of this Tribunal. The evidence will show that Jovic was the editor-in-chief of Slobodna Dalmacija for every relevant edition in this trial and he was responsible for his newspaper's actions. Beyond this various headlines and by-lines show Jovic's direct involvement in the contemptuous publications. The evidence relevant to these proceedings is 29 issues of Slobodna Dalmacija, four issues in November and 25 editions in December. The four November editions published Mesic's witness statement. The December editions published his closed session testimony. The evidence will show that the November editions identified the fact that Mesic had testified confidentially, and the November editions not only published the content of his witness statement but blurred the distinction between the witness statement and his courtroom testimony by referring to both of them as testimony. The OTP will show that the evidence in Mesic's witness statement is more or less the same as his closed session testimony. The slide currently being displayed on your screen comes from page 7 of the November 27th issue. On this page Mesic's witness statement is misleadingly advertised as testimony before the Court. The other highlighted quote on the screen is similarly misleading. These disclosures in November forced the Prosecution to file a motion asking the Blaskic Trial Chamber to issue an order against Slobodna Dalmacija to cease and desist any further publications of witness statements or testimonies. The Trial Chamber issued the order the same day on December 1st. The order directs Slobodna Dalmacija, the authors, and those responsible to stop publishing Mesic's statements or testimony. Now, the evidence will show that Jovic clearly received the cease and desist order shortly after its issuance, that he clearly understood its meaning, and he clearly decided to, and did, refuse to comply with it. On December 3rd, 4th, and 5th, Jovic features the cease and desist order on the front pages and the interior pages of Slobodna Dalmacija in a variety of articles but on those days does not publish the actual transcripts. On December 3rd, Slobodna declares on its front page that The Hague Tribunal has forbidden Slobodna Dalmacija to publish Mesic's testimony. The December 1 cease and desist order is printed in its entirety in this edition. The full transcript for all the arguments submitted for conducting Mesic's testimony in closed session is printed in the edition. The next day, on December 4th, Jovic, on the front page, declares in large bold font that he doesn't have any moral responsibility to The Hague. The front page questions whether Slobodna Dalmacija will receive an indictment from The Hague. The next day, December 5th, a front page headline features, in striking red font, a story about the court order, and the ban on the publication of the testimony. It quotes then ICTY spokesperson Jim Landale who says the order is actually a warning due to contempt of court. Then, on December 6th, Jovic publishes his decision, his decision to directly violate the order of the Trial Chamber. An article by Jovic trumpets the six reasons why Slobodna Dalmacija is publishing Mesic's testimony. In one of these reasons Jovic confesses to his commission of contempt. He says: We decided, notwithstanding the risk, to publish the whole contents of the testimony. And keep in mind, this is after three days, December 3rd, 4th, and 5th of Slobodna Dalmacija deliberating about the ban and the cease and desist order. In this article on December 6th, it proclaims in a huge dramatic headline that Slobodna reveals The Hague secret, and in another headline it expresses the bottom line of this case that it is publishing the transcripts of the secret testimony of the protected witness, Stjepan Mesic, before the Tribunal in The Hague in March 1998 in the proceedings against Tihomir Blaskic. And Slobodna Dalmacija, on December 6th, does exactly that. The first excerpt of Mesic's closed session testimony is published in the interior pages of that issue, and each and every day, for 22 days thereafter, the evidence will show that Jovic and Slobodna Dalmacija publish the complete transcripts of Mesic's closed session testimony, and on top of each of these articles states very clearly that the witness testified secretly. And not only do the interior pages of these issues publish the transcripts but the front pages of the ensuing issues continue to flaunt the direct and open challenge to the Tribunal. Slobodna Dalmacija again boasts on the front of its December 7th and 8th issues that it is publishing Mesic's secret testimony. The front page on December 7th flaunts the warning from the ICTY, that its irresponsible actions must have consequences, and it also publishes in the front page an actual excerpt of the closed session proceedings. Your Honours, the evidence will show that for each and every relevant issue Jovic is listed in Slobodna Dalmacija as the editor-in-chief. The Prosecution will present evidence that Jovic's acts violated two court orders. The first order is the Blaskic Trial Chamber's oral orders in March 1998, that Mesic's testimony was to occur in closed session; and as can be seen from the Sanction slide showing at the moment, Judge Jorda in the Blaskic trial pronounces the witness -- his testimony will occur in closed session, after having heard both written and oral arguments from the parties which occurred in private session. Mesic's name was never revealed in any open session testimony. The second order, of course, is the cease and desist order directed specifically at Slobodna Dalmacija and published by that newspaper. The evidence will establish that Jovic and Slobodna Dalmacija openly acknowledge these orders, both the oral order and the cease and desist order, and printed both of them in their entirety. So in conclusion, Your Honours, the evidence in this case proves beyond a reasonable doubt that Jovic as the editor-in-chief of Slobodna Dalmacija clearly, intentionally, and repeatedly violated the orders of this Tribunal and as such Jovic interfered with the administration of justice and was in contempt of this Tribunal, and we ask this Trial Chamber to find him guilty as charged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just to clarify, are you going to call evidence or are you relying on the documents that we've already admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: Based on the motion to admit documents, the Prosecution rests.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see. Thank you. So, Mr. Krsnik, it's your turn.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, truly I don't know what the indictment is based on. The Defence is about to show that everything that my learned friend, the Prosecutor, has just stated that the case is, in fact, the opposite. The Defence will show that my client, Mr. Jovic, did not knowingly and wilfully violate any orders of this Tribunal. Let's start at the beginning. I do know that the Chamber knows full well who Mr. Mesic is, but this begins a lot earlier, back in 1998, when Mr. Mesic held no political office. However, prior to that he had been holding all the highest offices in the former Yugoslavia as well. He was its last president, after which he became the first Croatian Prime Minister. After that, he became the president of the Croatian parliament. All the highest offices. After that, he retired, politically, so to speak, all the way until 2000, when he was elected Croatia's president, it's first president, in fact, after the late Franjo Tudjman. So what is it that we wish to say? This is a prominent politician, a prominent personality. Everything he does is bound to rouse interest on the part of Croatia's citizens, especially his voters. When this man testifies, he does not testify as a victim. He can't be subject to any sort of manipulation, threats, or whatever other reasons there are for granting protective measures to witnesses. However, I'm not about to embark on that now and start explaining the role of a protected witness, if indeed he ever was one. What we are about to show is that President Mesic never tried to keep it secret, the fact that he was a witness. We'll show his interviews, those in 1998 and those that he released when he became president. We shall show his public appearances in the printed media, the radio, and TV, to show that he never tried to keep this from the public eye. He confirmed that he had testified at this Tribunal for Slobodna Dalmacija, in fact. He told them on one occasion that he was not a secret witness and that he had nothing to hide. There are things that he said to Slobodna Dalmacija which seem to indicate that he was in fact happy that Slobodna Dalmacija had published his transcript, the transcript of his testimony. He said he was only afraid of one thing, forgery. He confirms that the first portion of what Slobodna Dalmacija published was, in fact, an accurate reflection of what he had said. But, Your Honours, that was nearly a year after he became president. Slobodna Dalmacija started publishing these pieces on the 29th of November, 2000, whereas Mr. Mesic was elected in January 2000. Why was this only published a year later? That is something that the Defence will show. We will show that the editors of Slobodna Dalmacija received three CDs, a set of three CDs, at their reception, anonymous tip-offs, regular mail from citizens who do not wish to declare their names. It's as simple as that. Mr. Jovic will explain that in his testimony today, Your Honours, and he will give you the whole truth, truthful account of what really happened. When the OTP showed Judge Jorda's picture on the screen, they said that in 1997 they had discussed the possibility of a private session. I'm saying that that is not true. Can Mr. Usher please help me to show the first page of the document that I have here on the ELMO. [In English] Can you put on the ELMO, please, no, on the ELMO. [Interpretation] We shall be distributing copies of this document in its entirety, needless to say, Your Honours. Something unbelievable happened. The Defence has a document, an official document, from this Tribunal from that very session. And, Your Honours, you were involved in the Rebic/Marijacic case. This was requisitioned as evidence. I'm trying to be very picky about my phrasing. Perhaps the OTP didn't know, but I submit they should have known. This is the official web page of this very Tribunal. If you scroll down the text, you will see that there is a discussion of whether Mr. Mesic will, in fact, testify or not. It was on this Tribunal's web pages. Anybody could have checked; anybody could have had a look. This was on the web page of this Tribunal throughout 1999 -- 1998, 1999, and I think the whole of the year 2000, I believe. Perhaps it still is. I don't know. I haven't looked. I'm not sure what the dilemma is here. I'm not sure what the secrets are that are involved. I am not sure why we are getting all this mumbo-jumbo from the OTP. In the year 2000, Slobodna Dalmacija publishes this order, it is debated and the indictment is expected in the year 2000, but it only arrives five years later. Did the OTP really believe that there was a violation here? [In English] I will show you the pages where Mr. Mesic is mentioned. Okay, first of all, in the page number 2 you have -- Mr. Harmon is asked for the private session and then Judge Jorda is going to the private session. And after it you have all session in -- this is the second page, and after it you have -- I will show you where Mr. Mesic is mentioned many times. You see now, Honourable Judge, in the middle of the page Mr. Harmon asked for the private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, yes, we see the private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And after it -- would you be so kind as to bring it back, please. And all private session in this transcript. And then in the page number 4 they are talking about Mr. Mesic many times and after it also. You will see: Need protection measure or not. [Interpretation] I will provide the entire document, however. I have it ready. It's right here. Before Mr. Jovic will start to testify, I do have a motion to submit because all these documents, you know, and the Registry is only open from 9.00. I need to ask your permission to have this distributed to the OTP and to the Chamber alike, not just this document in its entirety, but other documents, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. The fact itself that a lawyer who wasn't involved in that case is in possession of a document like that -- we're in private session and Lord knows what that means. How did I get this -- or rather, Mr. Jovic, who was the person who gave this document to me? I think the fact is self-explanatory, frankly. What causes me concern is Exhibit P7, OTP Exhibit P7, which has been admitted into evidence, but then it was already in the Rebic/Marijacic case by this Trial Chamber. All right, this was on the web page of the Tribunal. Of course he could have downloaded it back in 1998. Your Honours, a number of different Croatian newspapers, Vjesnik and Vecernji List, I'm just naming the two most popular ones and the two most widely read ones, especially Vecernji List published the testimony of Mr. Mesic in its entirety. Even in those dailies, and we're about to show that, Mr. Jovic is about to show you that, we have the source of this leak, if you like. It became a bit of an open secret, if you like. What happens? Nothing. In 1998 you have the whole statement, the whole testimony, of Mr. Mesic published in a number of different Croatian dailies. Mr. Mesic confirms that this indeed was the case, that he did testify at The Hague Tribunal. He confirms this for the sake of all the media. He's not keeping it under wraps or anything, and we have documents to show that. Well, what happens now? Firstly, in 2000, in the first three days, Slobodna Dalmacija merely reprinted the same text that was published back in 1998 because that was something, a statement that was given during the investigation stage, and only then did they in fact go on to publish a transcript from the trial itself. The OTP obtains this order. But what is noteworthy is that all the other most widely read dailies and weeklies in Croatia also published this transcript, magazines such as Globus, as well as a number of other dailies. But the only offices that actually received this order were Globus and Slobodna Dalmacija, not the other ones. There was a selection process at work there to keep this from being published, but the Defence believes there are other reasons at stakes here throughout. Even after this order other media continue to publish the transcript in parts or in whole. Five years have now gone by. The OTP is greatly concerned because they're taking five years for this. But the only person that they actually end up indicting is Mr. Jovic. From a marginal publication called Hrvatsko Slovo, three journalists and two editors -- by the way, they only ever print 1.200 copies of this paper, while Globus is published in 100.000 copies. They don't choose to indict the Globus people, but they do choose to indict the Hrvatsko Slovo people. So what is the last thing to happen? There is a motion for a joinder? I oppose this. You didn't accept my reasons, okay, so these journalists are given up, these charges are now dropped, but the same reasons for some reason do not seem to apply to Mr. Jovic. One of the journalists in relation to whom charges were dropped by this Trial Chamber has in the meantime violated six different orders of this Tribunal -- or rather, since 2000 -- or rather, between 2000 and 2005 -- or rather, between 2000 and 2006. The last order was issued in 2006. There was a spectacular police search all over Zagreb. They were trying to catch him. But that's all right. Let me not take this any further now. I believe the Defence has provided sufficient arguments, and we shall corroborate this by producing evidence, first of all, by having Mr. Jovic testify --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just for the record, you say that we didn't accept your reasons in relation to the application for joinder. The application for joinder was not granted; that's why we are here with Mr. Jovic today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is precisely what I said, that you did not accept the reasons for a joinder. I'm not sure what the transcript says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see. The reasons offered by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, that's right. You didn't accept the joinder, and after that the OTP gave up the indictment altogether. I do not wish to belabour this point, Your Honours. I believe the Defence will demonstrate and call into doubt all the reasons and grounds presented by the OTP. My last request, Your Honours, if I may be allowed to distribute to you and the OTP the motion that I was unable to file at 8.00 this morning because I -- it was explained to me that the motion can be filed only as of 9.00. I believe it would be of utmost importance for you to review the motion for the sake of the further proceedings in the course of the day, especially so because the motion contains evidence, written documents, which I wish to tender into evidence through Mr. Jovic, and I wish to use them. These are mostly newspapers, no other documents than that, and I wish to use them in the same way the Prosecutor did. These are interviews --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerson is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: I apologise. I'm presuming we're still in opening statements here, although it's getting a little blurry. But I wanted to raise an issue which is that we are looking to find the accused's exhibit list. We've -- we see that he has on his witness list indicated that Mr. Jovic might testify. We can't find an exhibit list. I would ask the Court to confirm that because I'm not quite sure that he's listed any exhibits. Therefore, if he's intending on introducing exhibits today, we would obviously object. He's not given us notice, he's had plenty of time. And apparently what it sounds like is that he is intending on introducing evidence that he has never notified us of before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Would you clarify, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, Your Honour. I confirm everything that Mr. Prosecutor said. I did not deliver the exhibit list to the Prosecutor before because I didn't have it. The list of exhibits consists only of the newspapers where Mr. Mesic and Madam Carla del Ponte gave their interviews in 1998, which support the case of the Defence. The 2000 interview by Madam del Ponte, which was published in all the Croatia mass media - and this will become clear from the evidence I adduce there - Madam Carla del Ponte informed the public of Mr. Mesic's testimony. I don't see where the problem is. These are short articles that have been translated. I -- it took me some time to find them because they were published in 1998, and I do not have as large a team as the Prosecution does. That's the first point. The second point is that Mr. Jovic in the past month was in a very difficult position, and I was unable to work with him at all. What's more, we didn't have a single pre-trial conference, and there was no occasion for us to discuss this. In a contempt case, I believe that this Trial Chamber may, proprio motu, decide in favour or against my motion. These are only four exhibits, namely four excerpts from newspapers, including this document that I showed on the ELMO here. This is the official Tribunal document, and I don't believe the Prosecution will be opposed to that. Therefore, in all five documents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, the Trial Chamber's order of the 15th did require you to file your exhibits and to provide copies to the Prosecution. But I understand that you are submitting that. Notwithstanding your lateness, you are saying that no -- there is no prejudice to the Prosecution in the light of the kind of exhibits that you are seeking to have tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I ask you: Where is the argument that you're trying to advance now, where is it referred to in your pre-trial brief?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We had only one preliminary motion, which did not contain an exhibit list of ours and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There must be a mistake in translation. My question relates to your pre-trial brief. You're advancing an argument here about the information already being in the public domain prior to the publication in November and December 2000. Where do we see reference to that in your pre-trial brief as part of your case?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I recall, without going into my pre-trial brief now, I don't believe I mentioned it there. I think you're right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because, as I wanted to say a moment ago ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would -- I would object to any admission of evidence without notice in any form to us, either on the exhibit list or in the pre-trial brief. It is -- it does prejudice us. I don't know what he's referring to. I haven't had any chance to review the documents, so I would object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll consider it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, explain the relevance to the case, the documents whose admission you're seeking.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Firstly, the document I showed to you on the ELMO has to do with Exhibit P7 that was admitted in the Marijacic Rebic case and in the Jovic case. This is in evidence, and the document I took from the public web page shows clearly that it wasn't a private session --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, the document -- the first -- the transcript is in the evidence in Rebic, but there was no -- there was no extract from a web page in the case of Rebic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course not, Your Honours. I do appreciate the work of the interpreters here, but there may have been a misunderstanding. The transcript from the private session was held before Judge Jorda in 1998. There is one transcript that the Prosecutor adduced as evidence and you admitted into evidence. The Prosecutor's argument, main argument, was that this was a transcript from a private session where protective measures were ordered in -- with regard to Mr. Mesic. The document that I would wish to tender into evidence, which is the same document, the same transcript, containing the entire private session but which was published on the official web pages of this Tribunal. I have it in my possession and I want everyone to see that. And I would wish to examine Mr. Jovic about it, about how he came by the document, because this very document was published in Slobodna Dalmacija. This very transcript that the Prosecution tendered into evidence and you admitted into evidence as P11 is the same one that I showed to you on the ELMO now. The Prosecutor gave you the same transcript, but not all of it was translated. I'm saying that this document that I have here was taken off the official web page of the Tribunal and had been there, available to anyone in the public domain, which is something we will later on support with further arguments. The interviews given to Vecernji List and Jutarnji List by Mr. Mesic in 1998 were interviews where he confirmed that he was testifying in two cases before this Tribunal. There was also the interview given to one paper by Madam del Ponte, where she confirmed that Mr. Mesic was a witness. I believe this is highly relevant. If you have a situation where the person publicly confirms this as a fact and then this very fact is used later on as the basis for an indictment, I believe that this is highly relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerson. Have you concluded, Mr. -- have you concluded, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I only wanted to say that these are four short articles that the Prosecutor can fully review in two minutes, if that's the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: First, Your Honour, the question of relevance I don't think is the appropriate question here. Defence counsel had ample time, including an extra week where he's very lucky his client wasn't issued a Bench warrant but was given a continuance. And he hadn't listed it at the prior trial date, and then he had an additional week and still hadn't listed any of these exhibits. So I would first say that the question of the relevance of the document isn't the primary concern of this Chamber; the primary concern should be fair notice and just -- fair notice to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, but it wouldn't be the first time that a Trial Chamber is faced with an application during a trial from a party to admit a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: I understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It happens all the time. And then the question of relevance is important.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: Fair enough. So these documents aren't relevant in this case, except perhaps maybe as mitigating circumstances to sentencing because Trial Chamber I issues an order to the paper and one of the exhibits that you've already admitted has arguments about the previous disclosures, and of course there were previous disclosures. They're part of that exhibit. But it's not up to a newspaper to decide whether or not an order that's directed specifically to them is valid, and that's his argument with these exhibits. So I would say that they should not be admitted in the case in chief of the trial, but they are potentially relevant for sentencing and that's where this Court should consider them. But they can't be relevant as to whether or not he violated a court order. They heard arguments, they heard arguments on these issues. An order was directed directly at the paper, he receives it, he publishes it, he says in the paper that, I've got the order, I'm going to violate it anyways. He then does it 22 straight days. That's the only issue; it's a violation of a court order. And Trial Chamber I had all of the circumstances in front of it when it made the decision to issue the cease and desist order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: This is the Trial Chamber's decision on your application, Mr. Krsnik. We'll mark the documents for identification. You should present copies to the Prosecutor so he can deal -- so he can see them and examine them. And during the evidence, we'll decide on their admission.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I only wish to say that my health condition is very bad. I have an ear infection, but I didn't allow it to prevent me from appearing here. But please have an understanding for me. It may not have been misinterpretation earlier on; it may just be me not taking things in fully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, we appreciate your being here, Mr. Krsnik, and we hope your health will improve. Mr. Krsnik, it's now for you to call your evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is that the only copy which was handed over to the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I omitted to say that this is the motion I completed yesterday. I suggested that two witnesses be called, but I knew you were going to be deciding on it proprio motu and that it will be in your hands to decide whether these additional witnesses are to be called or not. They were supposed to merely testify to some matters that the Prosecution presented in their pre-trial brief. But after the presentation of evidence and after we respond to the evidence presented by the Prosecution, we will discuss these further matters. One of the witnesses is the attorney-at-law, he's the public prosecutor, and the other one is the Prime Minister. And they will be examined on whether Mr. Jovic violated the order knowingly and wilfully, whether he was in a position to do that at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Those witnesses are present?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately they are not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, why, Mr. Jovic? The trial is set for today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I'm aware of all the consequences of that. Unfortunately I hesitate to offer any excuses in terms of us not having had enough time. Well, we did not have enough time because of Mr. Jovic's family situation. In the past seven days, I was able to obtain some of the relevant documents with the assistance of my investigators, and that is the reason why I submitted these documents today. However, I believe that Mr. Jovic's examination will show why I suggested that these two witnesses be called and why they should, in fact, testify in the interests of justice. This will also become clear on the basis of the arguments contained in the Prosecution pre-trial brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, we'll hear Mr. Jovic's evidence first and then we'll decide on your application.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I apologise if I'm asking too much, but could we be allowed a short break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let us carry on. We have lost a lot of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I call Mr. Jovic as a witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll be breaking at half past 9.00, Mr. Krsnik. Yes, let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Mr. Jovic, would you please present your CV briefly. I've already cautioned you about answering my questions as briefly and concisely as possible. So could you please let the Honourable Chamber know your personal background.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: I'm 56 years old, and all my career I was a journalist. Most of the time I spent in Slobodna Dalmacija as a political analyst, a commentator, and editor-in-chief in -- on two occasions. I also wrote for other Croatian papers. I published seven books on political matters. I was born in Imotski near Split. I am married with two sons, and I have two daughters-in-law.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: The second question, let us go into the merits of this case. Would you tell the Trial Chamber how long your newspaper and yourself have been following, as we like to put it, The Hague Tribunal matters and all the cases before it?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: I have to say that we have been following the activities of the Tribunal ever since its inception. Our assessment was that its activities were exceptionally important for our country and the region in general. We knew that whatever pronouncements the Tribunal would make would be very important, not only for the fate of individuals but also for the historical assessments and the people as a whole.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Pause, you should give a pause.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Please take it a bit more slowly.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: Either as a political commentator or as editor-in-chief, I can say that I have been continually following all the matters related to the activities of The Hague Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Let us go further into the merits of the case. When was the first time that you heard of Mr. Mesic having testified before the Tribunal in one or several cases and what year was that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: People first started talking about this back in 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Slow down, slow down.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: The first time it emerged that he wanted to say something about trials before The Hague Tribunal had to do with his evidence to The Hague investigators. I believe that this information was leaked immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Was this statement published in public media, the 1997 statement?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: The statement was published in at least three different newspapers in Croatia in Vjesnik, in Vecernji List, and in Slobodna Dalmacija, and the statement was profusely commented on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: My first question, it is your profession, after all, what sort of newspaper is Vecernji List, how many copies then and now? I suppose you still follow that. What sort of political commentary was that, written by whom, and how was this seen in the rest of the media?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: Vecernji List has for years been the most popular and the best selling daily in Croatia. For Croatian standards, the number of copies they print and sell every day is extremely high. The figure lies at about 150.000 copies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Daily?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I mean, every day. The political commentaries would normally be written by all the editors of all the dailies, and they were all, no exception, extremely critical of Stjepan Mesic's evidence. At the time, nobody had an inkling that he would one day be Croatian president.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Would you please be so kind and tell me this: After these comments made in these various newspapers, did Mr. Mesic release any interviews to any of the newspapers about his evidence, about his testimony?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: What I've just said is in relation to the period before he ever came to testify here, at least that was my conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Just a minute. Let me explain. You mean the trial that he testified at, right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I mean, the trial. Soon after he had appeared as a witness before The Hague Tribunal, a mere several months later, there were no longer any secrets about the fact that he had appeared as a witness before a Chamber of The Hague Tribunal, the ICTY. As you have also observed, counsel, he said it himself in the Feral Tribune and Vecernji List, on Croatian TV and radio. He said this unequivocally. He said that he had testified in The Hague. His statement was a contradictory one. The first time he said that he was not a secret witness of any kind. The next time he did say that he was a protected witness and so on and so forth. One thing that was crystal clear is that he had given evidence. His testimony, in part at least, and his identity were published in a number of other media. For example, on the web page of the Veritas documentation centre back in 1999, on the web page of certain news agencies, even on the web page of the London-based Institute for War and Peace.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Mr. Jovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Or, rather, if Mr. Usher could place this Feral Tribune piece. Your Honours, my learned friends, this is annex C, Exhibit 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: What I'd like to ask you is: Mr. Mesic testified on the 16th of March, 1998. Can you tell me what the date is on this Feral Tribune interview. Just the first three sentences and the heading, please.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: The heading --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: The date first, please.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: The 23rd of March, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: So this is only --

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, a matter of days after his evidence in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: The heading, please, the first two sentences, if you could please read that out.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: "I testified," says Mesic, "in the case against General Blaskic. I testified about circumstances that I am familiar with, but that I cannot explain further because I promised the president of the Chamber that I would not issue any comments on the course of the trial."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe we have already had all the relevant facts from this newspaper article translated. The next thing is annex D, Exhibit 2, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: If you could please tell the Court what this is about.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Well, the headline itself is self-explanatory. It says: "Yes, I testified in the Blaskic case, too."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Next, annex E, Exhibit 3. If you could please tell the Court, witness, what this is about. And the dates, please. The dates are very important.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: 21st of March, 1998, again, like the previous piece, 23rd of March. This is a Vjesnik piece. This is not an interview. This is a report in the newspaper itself saying that on that Sunday Stipe Mesic confirmed to the Croatian TV that he had during the previous week testified as a Prosecution witness in the case against General Tihomir Blaskic. Among other things, he spoke about an opinion offered by Ante Nobilo, Blaskic's counsel, saying that his testimony put the Defence in a very difficult position. This may lead one to conclude that Blaskic's counsel himself, Ante Nobilo, also published the fact that Mesic was protected witness, by saying, as we see, that it was Mesic's testimony that left the Defence in a very difficult situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: The last piece, the first sentence of the heading, annex F, Exhibit 4, what's this about?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: This is a later piece dated the 7th of April, 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Well, that was certainly before Slobodna ever -- right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is a brief interview with the Chief Prosecutor of the ICTY, Madam Carla del Ponte. In this interview she says -- or rather, this interview was published a little after Mesic became Croatian president --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Which --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Carla del Ponte --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Which document is this? I've only been given four that are all dated the 23rd of March, 1998. Is there a fifth one?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, let me check this. Your Honours, the mistake is ours. We wrote "Exhibit 4" and we said this was the 23rd. However, this is Jutarnji List and the date is the 7th of April, 2000. This is an important Croatian daily, Jutarnji List, selling over 100.000 copies. I think the interpretation is clear but that was our mistake. The error -- the original error was made in the annex. Our note was erroneous, for which I apologise.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to quote the following sentence from her interview. She says: "President Mesic is a friend of the Court" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerson is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: I understand that Defence counsel said that he had time to get translations of these. I have not been provided with that. Is there a translation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Second page of English on the top. "The Hague Prosecutor didn't want to comment on Blewitt's statement on secret indictments for Oluja. President Mesic is a big friend of Court." I can't read further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Do you have that, Mr. Ackerson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: If I could have a moment, Your Honour, just to kind of sort through the papers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Second page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: I do have it. I would like to point out, however, one of the arguments Defence counsel is making is that he didn't have enough time in order to prepare an exhibit or witness list, but clearly he had time enough to get a translation. I just want to make that point obvious to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will not grace that with an answer. Mr. Prosecutor knows full well that I can't even appear at this Tribunal if I don't have all the relevant translations, so that was obviously our priority.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I go on now?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: "Carla del Ponte claims Mesic was an important witness at one of our trials. He knows a great deal and it was wonderful talking to him." If you look at the overall context, it is clear that the Chief Prosecutor has the Blaskic trial in mind --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm struggling to find this in the English. Where is this in the English? All I have is a suggestion that the Deputy Prosecutor had said that Mesic is a big friend of the Court, that she repeated that there were no secret indictments.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe it wasn't translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it's good enough if it's translated -- it's not much use to me if it's not translated. I'm sorry, I haven't developed a facility for the Croatian language as yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that is the least of our problems. We have the original here. We can give it to the interpreters. They are here, after all. We're only looking at two sentences. We all have the Croatian original --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no, I apologise, Mr. Krsnik. I have actually found it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the lower half of the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: English page seems to have a problem with right margin. It does not show all the full line of the right margin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Your Honour. Even if you look at the original, the newspaper article, it's not very easy to read, is it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So you downloaded this English page from web page?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Sorry. [Interpretation] There's a portion of the text missing, that's the Vjesnik article, but here we have the whole article and the translation. And the bit that you were inquiring about is also missing, but I do not believe that the part read out by Mr. Jovic is missing; I think that has been translated in its entirety. It's halfway down the page in the Croatian and it's missing, so we couldn't have translated that into English. We translated what we received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Jovic, by the time this interview with Carla del Ponte was published, how long had Mr. Mesic been president for?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: For about three months.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Thank you. Sorry?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: I think he became president in January 2000 or possibly somewhat later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Let's move on to our main point. Can you please tell the Court when you, your own newspaper, or your board of editors, or your team of investigators, if you had one or set up one as part of your board of editors, I mean a team of investigative journalists -- so when did you first come across relevant documents pertinent to this trial or some other?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: It was during the election campaign when Mesic decided to run for president. He was overwhelmed with questions by journalists, by members of the public, various meetings. People wanted to know whether it was true that he had appeared as a witness against Tihomir Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I'm sorry for interrupting. You've been a journalist for over 30 years now. Is this good copy, as you journalists like to say? Is this something that was a subject of great interest at the time?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and it became even more interesting once Mr. Mesic had won the trust of the voters, he won the elections and became Croatia's president. Once he was elected, I as the editor-in-chief was suddenly in possession of what you define as great copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I called it great copy. This is journalese. I understand this is the term that you journalists use, right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: I received a set of three CDs. When we opened the parcel, we realised one of these was in Croatian and it was Stjepan Mesic's testimony in the Blaskic case. A second CD was the same thing in English. And a third CD contained the web page that you spoke about, the ICTY web page displaying information on a session where it was decided that Mesic would be awarded the status of a protected witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: So the third CD was what I precisely talked to the Court about, that was from the web page, from the official web page, of this Tribunal with this session with Judge Jorda presiding. The discussion was whether Mesic should be granted protective measures or not, right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: That was the third one?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Would you please tell the Court how this reached you. How does stuff reach you, journalists, in general?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: In a wide variety of ways. This particular parcel was addressed to the editor-in-chief and left Slobodna Dalmacija's reception. First it reached our porter, who gave it to my secretary, who left it on my table. And this is very often the case. This is normally how things reached me. There's no particular procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can we clarify when this was?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was my next question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was in January, possibly February, 2000. I'm afraid I can't be more specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Just one further clarification, please. Is this the established practice, for interested parties or citizens to send you anonymous parcels for you to publish?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is quite usual, especially when we're talking about things of great import. People don't know about this and they want to publish information on the one hand and keep the source secret on the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: All right. Let's move on to the main point. You told the Honourable Judge Bonomy that this was in January and February 2000. The first article appeared on the 29th of November, if I'm not mistaken. Why the ten-month time-lag?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: We had been thinking about this, pondering the possibility of publishing it for months, whether to publish and in what form.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Why was that? Why did it take you that long?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: Well, first of all, we weren't sure about the authenticity of the documents that we received. In the meantime, we had realised that some other newspapers, especially the newspaper that I had mentioned at the outset, had published certain portions that we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Let's try to keep this crystal clear. Let's try to clarify this. First you said you weren't sure whether the documents were authentic, right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Was there any way for you to check the authenticity of the documents received?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: The web page, the ICTY web page, was easy, because our own team of investigators was searching through the official web pages and they had already found the same document, which they saved on their own hard disk.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Your investigators monitoring the work of the Tribunal, right, and their web pages?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... can I ask whether you are going to come to the fact whether the accused, Mr. Jovic, still keeps those three CDs, whether he has it with him now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By all means, Your Honour. This is definitely something that requires clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Mr. Jovic, you see what the Chamber is interested in. I'm following the transcript, and whenever it seems to me that things are not clear, I press for further clarification. But before you answer this one, let's not forget about this. What I showed you today from the session presided by Judge Claude Jorda, the P7 that I showed you, Exhibit P7, is my understanding correct that your team of investigators found this same document? It was on your hard disk, and it was something that was downloaded from the official web page of this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the self same thing, that's what I was trying to say all along.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Now about Judge Kwon's question. The CDs, do you have those? What became of those? Tell us everything you know.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: I think copies were made of those. I don't have them in my possession. I didn't believe it would be necessary to bring them here, but I believe that they should be somewhere back home. I should have them somewhere in my files.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Could you send these to the Tribunal, should the Chamber so require?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: No problem at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it's half past 9.00. I think it's probably a good time for a break.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may just be allowed to complete this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerson, there are two matters that have been raised there that, it seems to me, should be capable of being verified. One is whether the Prosecutor did make public statements in 1998 about Mesic being a witness. The relevance of that to the later order is another matter, but it may be relevant to question of the closed session order. And the second thing that should be capable of verification is whether there was on a publicly accessible web site a transcript of his -- of the evidence -- or at least a transcript that indicates that Mesic was a witness here. And both of these tie in, in a sense, with a thing that's concerned me in this case, which is why nothing was done to draw this matter to the attention of the Trial Chamber when it was happening, why there was a great delay in raising this as a -- as an issue of contempt in relation to this particular accused. And I wonder if there is a relationship between these factors. I'm now beginning to question, in fact, whether the information had, in fact, been released publicly, whether inadvertently or not. And one has to ask whether that's why there was a delay in dealing with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: I'm happy to respond now to that question, Your Honour. It's up to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, but -- is that in the context of checking the other two matters which --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: I can actually respond presuming that those things are true, because I think the argument doesn't change that much, particularly with -- starting with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I would rather hear you later. I'm just mentioning the link and suggesting that you do check the other two matters to see if in fact we can cut through this and find out what the facts are much more quickly than it's likely to take by this exercise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: Right. I will -- over the break I will verify the assertions that are made by Defence counsel, but I do want to leave you with one clear assertion which is that no one -- none of these allegations none of these publications are asserting -- even on the web page of the ICTY are asserting that the content of Mesic's testimony was ever published. What they're talking about only is the discussions that were made regarding whether or not it should occur in closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But you immediately see the public interest issue that here's a man who's prepared to say: I'm not a secret witness at all, but then to hide behind an order while at the same time flaunting his identity as a witness. There's an issue to be addressed in relation to that, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: Well, I think that's -- I would disagree with that interpretation, and I think we should address that after the break. But I will -- I will attempt to verify both of those items.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just briefly, Your Honour. I said this at the outset. Exhibit P7 was tendered by the OTP. They believed it to be very important evidence. They claim that this was the final proof that the session was closed and that Mesic was granted protective measures, yet at the same time all of this was published on the internet. I apologise to my learned friend, but I don't think his answer was truthful. He used the very same document to persuade the Court or the Chamber of a totally opposite position. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll adjourn for half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Mr. Jovic, let us move on to disclosure now. Let me repeat the question. Why did you wait for nine months before publishing and what were the reasons behind your decision to publish what you indeed published?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: I decided to publish these documents at the time when they became an open secret, as it were. I had information that numerous papers were in possession of these documents, and it became a matter of professional competition as to who was to be the first one to publish them. Before my paper, the weekly Globus, started publishing the documents. We, as a daily newspaper, were able to take it more quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Could you please explain for the Trial Chamber what the weekly paper, Globus, is and how widely it is published?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: For years Globus has been the most widely read political weekly in Croatia, publishing between 50.000 to 100.000 copies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And how often is it published?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: Once weekly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Were they the first ones to publish the testimony of Mr. Mesic?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: They were the first one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: You said nevertheless that you had the advantage over them. Was it because you were able to publish the transcripts every day and they were only able to do it once weekly?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we were able to do it every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Was that the main reason why you decided to publish the documents? Did you compare the documents published by Globus with the material you had?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: Naturally. At first glance it was obvious that these were the self same documents. In addition to that, the identity of the protected witness was, by that time, widely known, as we have already shown. In these transcripts, Mesic was actually repeating what had already been stated in the investigative stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask the usher to place before the witness Prosecution Exhibit 11, tab 1 -- or rather, tab 2. Your Honours, you have a full translation of the document in the first binder, tab 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Would you please turn to tab 2. The title of the text is "Tudjman and Milosevic agreed on the division." Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Would you be so kind --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Your Honour, you have the pages in this big exhibit, Exhibit 11, tab number 2. And then you have all -- all translations you have it as pages number 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we found the copy. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Would you be so kind as to read the title of this other text on the same page, the last text, Stjepan Mesic in a TV show. Do you see that? Have you found that? Would you please read this subheading fully and could you state the date when this was said.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: The date is the 28th of November, the year 2000, where President Mesic states: "Slobodna Dalmacija has published something that actually suits me, provided they stay away from fabrications."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Carry on.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: "If, however, they engage in fabrications, only The Hague can put a stop to it. And as for who gave this statement to Slobodna Dalmacija, I will issue a public announcement soon, said Mesic."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Where did he say that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: According to Slobodna Dalmacija dated 28th November, he stated this in a TV show. This was an additional reason why we decided to publish this because the witness himself said that it suited him, of course provided that the transcripts are authentic. And based on what he says, one can conclude that he knows who the primary source of the transcripts is.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, not a TV show but a radio show.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Who knows?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: That Mesic knows who the primary source of the transcripts is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we set these documents aside. We will need them later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Can you tell us when you received the order and what happened next. How did the order arrive? How did you receive it? What happened?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: The situation is not as simple as Mr. Prosecutor explained it. Truth to tell, I received the order on the 1st of December, 2000 through a fax machine. We did not wish to disregard the order and what happened cannot be described as disregard for the Tribunal or as contempt of Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Pause there. Did you stop publishing the documents -- but please wait for me to finish my question so that the Trial Chamber can follow. You said that you received the order in the form of a facsimile on the 1st of December. Did you stop publishing the documents upon receiving the order or did you not? What happened next? If you did stop publishing the documents, why did you do that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: This is what I wanted to say, precisely, that we stopped publishing the documents in order to obtain the legal opinion in the Republic of Croatia and to decide, based on that legal opinion, whether we should feel bound by the order. As we had already started publishing the transcripts, it was difficult to stop publishing them, to make a pause. We informed the legal office of our paper and we also sent an inquiry to the general attorney's office. They had also received the order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: You want to say that the order was also sent to the public prosecutor's office in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and to the Ministry of Justice as well. The public prosecutor's office or the general attorney's office produced a written statement in reaction to that order wherein they established that the protective measures involved were addressed at the identity of the witness only and not at the contents of his testimony. They concluded that Slobodna Dalmacija had not violated these orders by publishing the transcripts, and that the identity of the protected witness had been revealed countless times by the witness himself. These were findings of the public prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Which one?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: The public prosecutor's office in Split.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Therefore of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Did you seek their opinion and did you ask for a written document to be produced?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I spoke with the municipal -- or rather, the public prosecutor in Split, who told me -- or rather, later on I found out that he had notified the main public prosecutor's office, that's to say of the Republic of Croatia, of this case. And among the -- those who were supposed to receive a copy was also the authority issuing the order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: You mean this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Do you have that document and can you present the Trial Chamber with it?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: I was looking for the document, but I managed to obtain only one page of it. As I was not able to obtain the document in its entirety, I did not bring it along. But I believe that by producing an order this Trial Chamber could easily get hold of the document. I only have its reference number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Could you give its reference number for the benefit of the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: I enclosed it there --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Give us the page you've got. Have we got the page that you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't have it here. I have it at home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because this is not the document in its entirety. Perhaps I'm mistaken. I'm not a good attorney-at-law. This Tribunal has never accepted partial documents, only documents in their entirety. I may have been wrong, but this was my experience before this Tribunal. The document exists in the file of the public prosecutor's office .

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, if you had any part of it you would expect it to be brought in at least a brief-case to the Tribunal. As you know, we were trying to have this case heard in the course of a day to cause as little inconvenience as possible to your client. And you seem intent upon causing him -- or he himself seems intent upon causing himself the maximum inconvenience.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I was not aware of the existence of this -- or rather, of the fact that this document was in possession of the witness. Had I known this, I would have brought it along, undoubtedly. As my client, Mr. Jovic, explained, he only had one out of five pages. He believed that in the form that he had it, the document was not relevant and he informed me of it only recently. But the document must be in possession of the public prosecutor's office and in possession of the ICTY. The reference number of the document is D-3-1/14814 ter. In this document, they state that Mr. Jovic was free to continue publishing this, and this was the position of the public prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, and the date was the 4th of December, 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: In addition to the public prosecutor's office, did you consult anyone else?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: We were seeking ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerson, can you help us in tracking down this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]. I mean, I can make attempts to do that, but one of the problems, you know, with adding documents without notice is I don't have a chance to verify. I don't know if this document exists. We are adducing evidence about a document that's not in front of the Court. We have no idea of its authenticity. The public prosecutor's office, I mean, I can attempt to do that but I have no clue whether it actually exists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I know you have no clue, but it would assist us if you can, because counsel says that he thinks it's in the -- that your office may have a copy of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: I will attempt to do that, Your Honour, but I would submit anyways it's irrelevant because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm not sure it's irrelevant. It may go to the issue of mens rea and intent. We're not deciding that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: Well, we're actually deciding on the probative value and the relevance of a document because you have to make that determination whether to admit it without it being listed as an exhibit, and that is the basis that the Court is deciding these decisions on. I mean, I can just tell you that you could give any number of legal opinions from any variety of sources, but the fact is you, this Trial Chamber, issued an order, and he's not entitled to get an opinion from Greenland or the United States or anywhere else to say that that's wrong. Right? He has -- if this Tribunal has the authority to issue this order, that has to be respected on its face. And what you're entertaining, I would submit, Your Honour, is that he has a right to get a second opinion from another legal entity to question the validity of your court orders, and that can't be. And so I would say it's irrelevant. I would say it's irrelevant and it's not probative of an issue in this trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may be allowed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really don't understand the point the Prosecutor is trying to make. This is not true. For the Republic of Croatia to be able to cooperate with the ICTY, it had to pass a constitutional law to that effect, and that also applies to any country in the world. The constitutional law provides specifically for the cooperation between Croatia and the ICTY, and this was done by Italy, France and a number of other countries, except for the United States, who refuse even to recognise the ICC. And it will be interesting to see if such an order were to be addressed to the United States what their response to that would be. Therefore, it is highly relevant for every citizen of the Republic of Croatia to inquire with the relevant institutions, which Mr. Jovic did. He addressed the public prosecutor's office in charge of prosecution in that country, to which this Tribunal sent an order to take certain steps. And this particular institution says that it cannot take any steps because Mr. Jovic is not engaging in any criminal activity. And this position is also notified to Mr. Jovic. According to our information, the same piece of information, the same document, was sent to the ICTY and it has to be here. That was why I invited that municipal public prosecutor to come before the Tribunal as a witness and confirm this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Proceed, Mr. Krsnik. We'll not make any determination on that at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Mr. Jovic, did you apply to the public prosecutor's office only or did you approach any other institutions?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness's microphone is ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We also sought the opinion of the government of the Republic of Croatia. The government stated that as far as this case involving the issuance of the order was concerned, the public prosecutor's office was competent to deal with this. The then-Deputy Prime Minister and the head of the office of the Republic of Croatia for Cooperation with ICTY, Mr. Goran Granic, stated that this was not the matter within the jurisdiction of the ICTY and that the general public was entitled to know it all. To me, as a professional, the position of my professional association, the Croatian Society of Journalists, is also relevant. The association, having met -- or rather, its main board having met decided that this was the case of censorship of the media and that the public is entitled to know every single piece of information. As I said, Mr. Mesic himself stated that he was going to ask for the protective measures to be lifted and that he was not opposed in any way to the publication of these transcripts. These positions faced me with a dilemma as to whether to stop publishing the documents or not, and ultimately I made the choice I did, the reasons for which I conveyed in the heading that was quoted by the Prosecutor himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: You have P11 before you, Mr. Jovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Did you, Mr. Jovic, publish in December as a reason for publishing the articles the terms of the legal advice and the government comment that you've just referred to?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And please let the witness answer the question rather than you, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We did not directly state that as the reason for publishing the transcripts, but we were taking account of this, by all means, when deciding to carry on publishing the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And secondly, did you publish as a reason for publishing the evidence the fact that Mr. Mesic said that he was going to ask for the measures to be lifted and that he had no objection to their publication?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think so. I think this was clearly indicated as one of our reasons to publish these transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No doubt Mr. Krsnik will draw your attention to the passages that make that clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Did you establish, Mr. Krsnik, how long after the advice from the prosecutor's office was the publication made?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Six days. Six days later. I've all the evidence. This is part of the Exhibit 11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... for the witness to give that evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was just about to embark on all this evidence contained in Exhibit 11. It says that everything was published. The government's position, Goran Granic's position, Mesic's testimony, the reasons for publishing it, it's all right there. I was just about to take that up. By your leave, I would like to embark on Exhibit 11, tab 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Have you got that, sir? I just want tab 8.
