utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: Just while we have this break, I just wanted to make sure that the record is clear that I'm objecting to the testimony that's being adduced to this information, the documents that we're referring to which are not in front of this Court, on the basis, first of all, that they were not provided to the Prosecution beforehand; secondly, on my previous relevance arguments, but I didn't object as we -- each time a question was asked because it would be tedious, but I just want to make the record clear that I'm objecting to the whole issue that we're adducing evidence on. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is evidence admitted by the Court. I'm just using it. It's been admitted. It's nothing new, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Mr. Jovic, do you see your own piece, which you signed as Josip Jovic, editor-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, you will see that only a small portion of it has been translated. I'm not sure if we have a full translation. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Sir, were all the reasons explained here, the reasons that Judge Bonomy was just asking you about?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the principal reasons anyway. You see those six items.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is this the publication of the 6th of December?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And this is the one that says clearly that you know that you're breaking an order of the Tribunal. It says: "Viewed from a legal point of view, this Tribunal has the competence for such conduct." That's the one we're looking at, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. That's a small portion that's been translated, but you have a full translation of another piece where Mr. Jovic explains --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But it shows clearly that he understands that the Tribunal has authority, has made a competent order, and he's defying it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's not the way I see it, Your Honour. All it says is that there's a certain amount of risk involved, but after all the advice that he had obtained - and he goes on to explain this - despite the risk, despite the possible risk, he still decides to go ahead and publish it, and you have the six items there, the reasons why.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And you're going to show that one of them refers to the advice he's got?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In English page I can note Josipovic's opinion and Granic's comment are all there in volume 1, binder 1, Exhibit 11, tab 8, we have English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, quite right. I wanted to tackle one thing at a time, but I was waiting for your questions. All these opinions were published, the opinion of the government, the opinion of the Deputy Prime Minister, the opinion of the Professor Josipovic. All these were published beforehand. Eventually Jovic used all these and summed them up in his six points.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I would like to be directed to the part which -- so that I'm clear in my mind about these various -- where does Granic say: This is not a matter for the ICTY?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm at it, Your Honour. I'm at it. This is Exhibit 11, tab 7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I've got the document. Show me the passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "The public has the right to know everything. This has nothing to do with The Hague."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What page?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]. Is it not one of the titles, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Yes, yes. [Interpretation] Yes, yes. [In English] And then -- [Interpretation] No, that's the actual headline, the title.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I've got the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just -- you must ensure that the Chamber is following your evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Clear enough. Needless to say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We're on tab 8. We're on the 6th of December, I thought. Are we now on the 5th of December?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Now we're on the 5th of December.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We're looking for something which expresses a legal opinion, I thought. That's what I'm looking for. I mean, I don't want this man's assertions about not liking The Hague. I want to know where is this legal opinion that's referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: If I can just assist the Court. In tab 7, there's -- there's a one-page English translation of the cover and then the very next page, which is a five-page English translation, there is an article by Mr. Granic and he does express a number of legal opinions, starting on -- and it's at the bottom marked "page 1 of 5." It's at the top marked ET0465-8075, 1 of 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And what's the opinion he's expressing?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: Well, I would direct your attention to the middle paragraph that starts with: "President Stipe Mesic didn't ask The Hague Tribunal for any protection," including with the sentence where he says: "However, as a protected witness he is not allowed to talk about his testimony in public." That's the opinion expressed by Mr. Granic in this article.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not only that. He goes on to say that Mr. Mesic has nothing against his testimony being published. That's what Goran Granic claims. Jim Landale, the spokesperson for this Tribunal, in that same piece in fact, claims that the order is a warning about a possible violation; a warning, nothing more. That's what Jim Landale says, because he was contacted, too, the journalists did. And then in the same piece you have the Croatian Journalists' Society. This is in one of the boxes. The editorial board of the Croatian Journalists' Association met on Wednesday or will meet on Wednesday and will publish an announcement. That's what Mr. Jovic referred to a while ago. Goran Granic's principal thoughts are very clear. "President Stipe Mesic did not require any sort of protection from the ICTY. He has nothing against his testimony before the Tribunal being made public."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Go ahead and read it. Turn your mic on, please.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: Granic's statement, the second-to-last passage: "The publishing of transcripts is not something for The Hague Tribunal to decide on. I don't know why the Tribunal puts itself in that sort of situation. Now that the whole thing's become public, though, the best course of action would be to allow the public to inspect everything." And I must say, Goran Granic is not just anybody. He is the number one person in Croatia at the time for cooperation with the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: What about his position?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: He was the Deputy Prime Minister and the head of Croatia's government office for cooperation with the ICTY.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Can we please now move on to the government announcement. This is Exhibit 11, tab 10. What does the Croatian government say on the 8th of December, 2000? There's just a headline; unfortunately, we don't have the main body of the piece. What did the Croatian government say? Who was in charge of deciding on Slobodna Dalmacija and the pieces it published?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, that is the front page. There's this heading in a grey box: "Government communique upon receiving order from The Hague Chamber." There's a translation of that. It says: "The public prosecutor has jurisdiction over anything published in Slobodna Dalmacija." This is very concise and, above all, crystal clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours, I can't find this particular passage that counsel has referred to. If he could direct me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's right here. It's Exhibit 10, the translation is right there. Exhibit 11, tab 10. The heading is here and the translation is right here. You have the translation right there. There's no need for you to go through the binders. Exhibit 11, tab 10, the box right there and the translation next to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Date is 8th of -- December 8th, 2000.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So you are referring to the passage which says: "Government issues statement following the order of the Trial Chamber"?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. [In English] "State attorney's office has jurisdiction over the articles in Slobodna Dalmacija."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's stating the obvious, if I may say so. It doesn't follow, for a minute, from that that the Tribunal here doesn't have jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies, Judge Bonomy. Don't get me wrong. It's precisely the opposite. It's not The Hague that has jurisdiction over that; the conclusion is different. It's the state attorney of the Republic of Croatia; they are supposed to grant permission, and they published their own position. They clearly said that Mr. Jovic was not in violation of any law in the Republic of Croatia and that he was free to go on publishing those. And that's what we said earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That may well be an accurate statement of their view of the rule in Croatia, but we are talking about a Tribunal here with international jurisdiction, whose orders have been defied. And there's no reason why more than one court in the world can't have jurisdiction over an issue. The statement that Croatia has jurisdiction doesn't imply that this Tribunal has no jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but it must be a knowing violation. Mr. Jovic is a journalist; he's not a lawyer. That's why he asked around. He did his best. He refrained from publishing for six days. He asked around and everybody was telling him that there was no violation at all. If he'd been told that he was in violation, he wouldn't have published, but the public prosecutor told him he was not in breach of any laws or regulations and was also clearly told that this was nothing for the ICTY. This was not a matter under ICTY jurisdiction and he was not doing anything that could have been viewed as impermissible. And that is why the witness decided to publish this eventually. And the state president is, after all, the most protected person in any country. One thing that I would like to draw the Chamber's attention to is just something that I might be in danger of forgetting about later on. Exhibit 11, tab 6 --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Mr. Jovic, let me ask you this: Did the Globus weekly receive the same order as you?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was made public, both Globus and Slobodna Dalmacija at the same time received the same order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Could you please read what's inside that box over there. The heading: The Globus editor-in-chief, Davor Butkovic, what does he say there, and what's the date?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: The 4th of December.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: The Globus editor-in-chief says: "Globus will not comply with The Hague order banning the publication of transcripts of protected witnesses. If Globus deems a document to be of relevance to the public, it will be published."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Can you please read on.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: "In a statement to the HINA news agency, Butkovic emphasised that with no final court ruling, The Hague Tribunal or any other institution, is unable to order anyone about telling them what to publish and what not to publish because this would fly in the face of freedom of the media" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber has difficulty locating the document. Tab 6, 4th of December, we have got as Slobodna Dalmacija, not Globus.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's most certainly Slobodna Dalmacija, but the Globus editor-in-chief made this statement to Slobodna Dalmacija. What has just been read was indeed written there. This is what the Globus editor-in-chief is saying to Slobodna Dalmacija.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But there's no translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Yes, there is. Yes, there is. It's Exhibit 6, there's a translation of that. What we have no translation of is in the big exhibit, but what there is in the binders has been fully translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you found that, Your Honours? [In English] Page number 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The position of Slobodna Dalmacija's editing chief, Davor Butkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Yes, Globus editor-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: "I will not obey the order."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: What about Globus? They received the order but they went on publishing, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: What about Mr. Butkovic, does he stand indicted?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that was a very leading question you asked about Globus. I'm not sure I know the answer from what's been said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I agree, Your Honour. I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And I don't think -- Mr. Jovic doesn't sound as though he knows.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't sound as if I know what? You mean if he actually went on publishing? I can't confirm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Jovic, you received the order not to publish, but you went on publishing. Why was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because based on everything that I have said so far, I was misled into believing something that was erroneous. I had received contradictory instructions and interpretations. I was not certain, nor indeed am I now, whether the ICTY can issue orders to me that affect my right to enjoy freedom in informing my readership.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What was the misleading information that you received?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The government position that was declared; the position of Goran Granic, the Deputy Prime Minister; the interpretation offered by the state attorney; the position put forward by the Croatian Journalists' Association; the positions of many highly qualified lawyers, politicians and holders of public offices; the positions put forward by some international professional associations, such as the European Journalists' Conference; the Reporters Without Borders; even some rulings of the European Court in similar cases, of which I only have indirect knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Did you not accompany your publication with a statement that you knew that the publication was in violation of the order of the Tribunal but you would publish nonetheless?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Quite obviously. But I stated the reasons that led me to start publishing. I was by no means clear whether the ICTY had the power to issue to me such an order; I think that is a matter for debate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Just in order to simplify what Judge Robinson has just asked you, did you actually know that you were publishing something that you were not allowed to publish?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Well, explain, that is what you were just asked.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: I was facing a legal dilemma because of contradictory accounts that I had received and contradictory interpretations. Based on some of the information I had obtained, I was not bound in any way to follow the order, and the only thing that opposed this interpretation that I was aware of at the time was the order itself. It's quite obvious, I flouted the order. But what is not clear is as a citizen of the Republic of Croatia am I duty-bound to follow that order. I am not a resident of Greenland; I am a resident of the Republic of Croatia which has its own laws, its own constitution. There is something called the UN declaration of human rights, founders of this very Tribunal guaranteeing to all the freedom to spread and publish information. There is the European Union Convention on Human Rights which addresses the same entitlements with no interference from the authorities. That is stated unequivocally. It's not as simple as it may seem. I am an intellectual. I take into account the political circumstances. I take into account the body of law relevant for these areas, human rights on the one hand and freedom of information, freedom of press on the other. I must take all these into account, as opposed to just one order taken as an absolute yardstick that can, under no circumstances, be challenged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Jovic, as I think you well know, all the instruments to which you refer on freedom of the press have qualifications in relation to court proceedings. I just make that point to the extent that it is relevant. Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. Jovic. I urge you to focus a bit. I will reiterate the question put to you by Judge Robinson. What were the relevant opinions put forth by the agencies of the government of the Republic of Croatia and professional peers? Was there a single opinion that went in favour of obeying the order issued by the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: No, the position --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let's hear Mr. Ackerson. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: The question's been asked and answered. The issue is well in front of this Chamber now. I don't think we need to rehash it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I agree, Mr. Krsnik. That's a matter that you can raise in your address.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may be allowed to add something. Within the witness protective measures, there was another matter that led me to doubt --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm sorry. The witness at the moment is now giving a speech, he's not responding to a question, and I would object to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll hear what you have to say briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is merely the continuation of my answer. Within the witness protective measures orders, it is clearly stated who the measures are addressed at, the Defence counsel, the Prosecution, but by no means does it address the journalists. Therefore, the order states the parties that were to obey and comply with the order. As a journalist, I am not part of the judicial mechanism; I am part of the public domain, and I cannot protect any judicial secrets from myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Finally --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's an interesting comment, because that's you asserting that no order of a court, whether it be in Croatia or here, which provided for closed session testimony would apply to you as a journalist. You would defy it in -- if it was made by a Croatian court or by this Court, if you thought it in the public interest.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot categorically answer the question, but I would probably take a similar course of action.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Perhaps not much more to be said, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honour, I wanted to show the Trial Chamber the relevance of the circumstances existing in the Republic of Croatia. That was why I wanted to show you Exhibit 11, tab 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: But now I have to ask Mr. Jovic whether he knows who Mr. Ivo Josipovic is.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: Ivo Josipovic is a renowned legal expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Will you tell us what his occupation is?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: He's a professor at the faculty of law, and I believe that international law is his specialty and he has dedicated the past years of his professional work to the ICTY.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Can you tell what he stated for Slobodna Dalmacija on the 6th of December, 2000 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: Sorry for the interruption. I suspect that this is going to be the same line of inquiry about Mr. Jovic receiving another opinion that differed from the court order. It may be that it's other testimony, but if they are going towards that line of testimony about soliciting different legal opinions that were contrary to the court order, I would object. And I think it's already been asked and answered. The issue's out there, and it doesn't need to be addressed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Professor Josipovic is the highest authority in the field of the ICTY in the Republic of Croatia, and I believe that my learned friend from the OTP will fully agree with this. And his legal opinion given to a journalist who was never before the ICTY, who cannot view matters the way you do or I, of course this can be a matter for mens rea. The person involved is the president of the state. Imagine if you had the president of the United States testifying about Iraq before this Tribunal. I believe that this is a matter of universal human rights.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll hear it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Mr. Jovic, please read out this small passage which was translated into English, that's Exhibit 11, tab 8.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: This is the first case --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Please, first the headline.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: "This is the first case where the ICTY issues a special order to the media of a country. Formally and legally speaking, this Tribunal does not have the authority to do that. However, any Court ruling, including this one, is subject to criticism and scrutiny. If it is established that no longer the reasons are in place for" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let's hear Mr. Ackerson, he's on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, there might be a question of translation, because the English translation which is in tab 8, which is the second page in that tab, and at the bottom it's marked "page 1 of 6," and the last paragraph which has a bold caption which says: "Confidentiality can be lifted," Mr. Jovic is reading the same in Croatian, and I don't know whether his version is more accurate or the English translation in writing what you have here. But the English translation in writing says: "Legally speaking, the Tribunal is entitled to do such a thing," and Mr. Jovic, I believe, just said that the Tribunal was not entitled to do such a thing. I don't know which is accurate, but I think that needs to be resolved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It certainly does. What is the original?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The original reads just as Mr. Jovic has read it out. And I will tell you now that for me, having worked before this Tribunal for eight years, I can say that this isn't the first time that the translation provided by the OTP is not accurate. I apologise, this may indeed be a genuine error, but there were many such errors. I believe the text reads the way Mr. Jovic read it out here, and -- but this can of course be confirmed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Let's ask the witness to read it and we'll have the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: Or, Your Honour, could I suggest that we put the original Croatian version on the screen and have one of the interpreters read it. And I would be satisfied with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: I don't know that Mr. Jovic is qualified to actually translate that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: It's in the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's on the screen, yes. Can I ask the interpreter to translate that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "Legally speaking, the Tribunal does have the authority to do that." It was the interpreter's mistake. Apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, let us -- let's hear that again. You're saying that the correct translation is "legally speaking, the Tribunal does have the authority to do that"?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't you ask Mr. Jovic to read the passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Yes, I was asking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And once again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Mr. Jovic, please, could you read out the entire text, including the headline.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: Headline: "Confidentiality can be lifted. This is the first case" --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Please take it slowly.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: " -- that the International Criminal Tribunal is sending a special order -- is issuing a special order to the media in a country. Formally and legally speaking, the Tribunal does have the authority to do that."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Carry on.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: "However, any ruling of the Tribunal, including the instant one is subject to criticism and scrutiny. If it is established that the reasons why some of the material were declared confidential no longer exist, the Tribunal may change the ruling. Such a course of action should be taken if the reasons of safety and security no longer exist and which would prevail over the clear public interest to learn certain details from a court proceedings, Professor Josipovic said."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: My follow-up question to that is: Did Mr. Mesic agree with the publishing and did he agree with the fact that the confidentiality should be lifted once he became the president?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: We --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: Objection --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- said on several occasions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: Unless Mr. Jovic spoke directly to -- or has first-hand knowledge and spoke directly to Mesic, it's speculation. It's asked whether Mesic agreed, and that's hearsay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I agree. What would be the basis of your knowledge, Mr. Jovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may be of assistance. We discussed this. This is Exhibit 11, tab 2. We've already read that part. We don't to waste any more time. Here Mr. Mesic is in agreement with the publishing of these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's not my understanding of this particular passage, Mr. Krsnik. I thought that he was claiming that only The Hague Tribunal could stop Slobodna Dalmacija.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the documents published were a forgery or a fabrication, and if such fabrications are indeed published, then the only party that can put a stop to that is The Hague --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, could you point the passage to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This can be found in the subheading in Exhibit 11, tab 2 -- [In English] Page number 4 in Exhibit 2 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Oh --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exhibit is 11, tab 2, page 4. And this is the text in a box. You have the English translation of it where Mr. Mesic states: "Slobodna Dalmacija has published something that actually suits me, provided they stay away from fabrications." I was reading the original now, but let me look at -- therefore, the main headline is: "Only The Hague Tribunal can stop Slobodna Dalmacija." It is clearly stated here that The Hague Tribunal can put a stop to that only if his testimony is fabricated, that only in that case would he seek protection from the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, excuse me for being skeptical about your translation, Mr. Krsnik, in view of what we've just recently experienced. I think I would like you to identify the passage in the Croatian language and ask Mr. Jovic to read it. Because we don't have an English translation of the part that you're referring to -- oh, we do?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Yes, you have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I do -- we do have it. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, would you bring your examination-in-chief to an end in about five to ten minutes. Bear in mind that we have to conclude by 1.45, and there is cross-examination to take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By all means, Your Honours. I meant this to be my last question for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Could you please briefly answer my questions. The first question: Do you know whether the trial against Blaskic had ended with a final decision before you went on to publish the documents?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: The trial was closed and a judgement was rendered for Mr. Blaskic. With the publication of these documents, we could in no way affect the administration of justice in these proceedings, as opposed to the charges against me, which state that I interfered with the administration of justice.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Could you please refrain yourself from commenting.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: The documents were published after the rendering of a final decision in that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: We said this several times, but I will ask you again. Do you know how long Mr. Mesic had been president by then and what sort of protection had been afforded him?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mesic has now entered his second term of office, which in Croatia lasts five years, and he's probably the most protected person in the Republic of Croatia. The publishing of these transcripts could not pose any physical threat to him. Judging from the election results, it inflicted no political damage on him either.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Now that you mention the political damage, can I ask you the following. Why were protective measures sought during that famous private session, the transcript of which we obtained from an official web page, do you know that at all?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... to answer that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, on the basis of the transcript. If he read it, there Prosecutor Harmon clearly explains why the protection is sought. And if he read the document, he would be able to know; if he didn't read it, he doesn't know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is one place where it reads --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You must not speak when counsel is on his feet. Mr. Ackerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: I would object to the question as asking for a legal opinion from this witness, and I think the document speaks for itself, as Defence counsel has stated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We can read it also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yeah, we can read the document ourselves. Mr. Krsnik --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was what I wanted to get from the witness, whether he was familiar with the document and whether he knew why protective measures were sought, nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Why did he ask for the protective measures? Was he well-known?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: The protection was motivated by political reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: That's all?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: And the danger of potential political abuse.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: My final question. Exhibit 11, tab 5 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just before you ask it. This is your view. In other words, you say that the Prosecutor was misleading the Tribunal. Is that right? Because political reasons weren't the reasons given for the application.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I remember, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm trying to locate the place where this is clearly stated in the document. However, you have the document before you, you will be able to read it, and you will see that these were the only reasons put forward by the Prosecution during that session in support of their request for protective measures, the threat of political manipulation. This was sought by Prosecutor Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Was this document published in Slobodna Dalmacija?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is there an answer to that question? A question was asked of you, Mr. Jovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Did you publish this document in Slobodna Dalmacija?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: The entire transcript was translated into the Croatian language and was published in Slobodna Dalmacija in its entirety. And I'm referring to this session where protective measures for witnesses were being decided upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, may I take you back to an earlier part in the proceedings today when Judge Bonomy asked the witness a particular question. It was immediately after I had disallowed a particular question on an objection raised by the Prosecutor and the witness wanted to volunteer something and I allowed him to volunteer something. Following what he said, Judge Bonomy then said to him: Your position then is tantamount to saying that notwithstanding an order made by this Court or any court, you would publish it, provided you thought it was in the public interest. And the witness said: Yes. Now, that seems to me to be a very damaging answer to his case, and in fact inconsistent with the way I thought the Defence was being wrong, which is that is accused is saying he published but not in knowing violation. But the answer that he gave to Judge Bonomy would seem to suggest that he's a man who thinks he has a right to publish, notwithstanding an order from a court to protect particular evidence, provided he thinks it's in the public interest. So I'm allowing you -- giving you an opportunity to have that clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, you're quite right to have taken it that way. I think everything we've been saying today does not point in that direction, and I'm glad to have my attention drawn to that by you. Thank you very much, indeed. I think Mr. Jovic had been given a chance to explain his entire position because I was he was crystal clear. He had listened to advice given by legal experts. They convinced him that he was not in violation of any court orders. I think he has spent the morning trying to explain that. But I think we best hear that from Mr. Jovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Mr. Jovic, you heard the question from Judge Robinson and Judge Bonomy. Please explain that for us.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: I tried to describe the situation that I found myself in. I wanted to stop publishing the transcripts. I wanted to comply with the orders, and that's why I took so much time to consult with people. I will not go through all of it again. But other sources offering other interpretations were telling me that in this particular case on account of all the circumstances surrounding it, I was in no way bound to comply with the court order in full. I do not knowingly, wilfully, and particularly not spitefully, violate the order of this Tribunal. Maybe I just decided to lend credence to other interpretations that were offered to me at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How long will you be, Mr. Ackerson? We have to stop at about 1.30 because one of our members, in fact, has a hearing this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: An hour or less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Then we'll adjourn until 12.00 and then we'll have your cross-examination when we return.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Jovic. First I want to just clarify one point before we begin the examination. You said you're an intellectual and that as the editor of Slobodna Dalmacija you followed the trials here at ICTY very closely. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: You could call it second-hand experience, not first-hand experience. I follow coverage in the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: Do you -- in your experience as the editor of a major newspaper in Croatia, you certainly know the difference between a witness statement and in-court testimony, do you not?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I -- I'm afraid I would not be able to really define the distinction between witness statements and in-court testimony, which can also be a witness statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: That's --

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know the difference, apart from the purely formal difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: Narrow enough. I want to make sure that we're clear on this point before we proceed because I'm going to refer to both of them. Do you recall that you and I were going to meet to have a witness statement but that was not in court. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: Correct. We had a meeting. I'm not sure if this is correct, it was at a stage where the investigations were still underway. And then there was an agreement to meet again, but this never materialised.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: Mr. Jovic, just try to keep your answers simple, and if you need to clarify you can do that. But the point is that we were going to meet in Croatia not in court, the purpose of which was I was going to take a statement from you. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: I assume so, yes. I was prepared to give that statement. My lawyers wanted a postponement so that we might be given a chance to prepare for any questions that you might ask, and as far as I know that was all right by you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: Today you're testifying here in front of three Judges. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: There were no Judges before, correct, when we previously met?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: The investigators were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: Correct. Do you understand the difference now between an out-of-court statement that you would have made to investigators and to me and your testimony here in court today in front of Judges?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: Well, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: There are procedural differences, essential ones if you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And the form of the statement -- strike that question. The relevant issues in Slobodna Dalmacija that this Court is deciding on here today are 29 issues in November and December of the year 2000. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: Four of the issues were published in November, starting with November 27th?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: 25 issues were published in December, starting on December 3rd?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: The four issues in November published the witness statement of Mr. Mesic; isn't that correct? Not his in-court testimony but his witness statement.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: I assume that was what I was supposed to tell you in Zagreb, wasn't it? Yes, that was a witness statement, out of court, if you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: The simple question I'm asking you is that what you published in November in four issues in Slobodna Dalmacija was Stjepan Mesic's witness statement, not his in-court testimony.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: Let it be that way. I agree with you. I agree with the phrasing. But I must add we actually copied that statement from Vjesnik, another daily, as an introduction to --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: I didn't ask that question, though. I would ask you to answer my questions and your counsel will have the opportunity to clarify. Okay. The publications --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]. Mr. Krsnik is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, please, my client is not used to courtrooms. I think this is the very first time in his life. Can you please ask the Prosecutor to try to be less strict with the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, if he is doing anything improper, we will see to it that he's stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: Mr. Jovic, the four issues in November, Slobodna Dalmacija published witness statements. The 25 issues -- strike that. The 22 issues, starting with December 6th published Mr. Mesic's in-court testimony, the transcripts of his testimony, yes?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: And you had mentioned earlier here that in 1997 Mr. Mesic's statement had been published -- I'm sorry. Are you having trouble hearing? Is there a problem with your hearing, Mr. Jovic? Are you not getting the translation?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: There was a glitch, but it's fine now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: You had referred in your testimony here earlier to the publication of Mr. Mesic's statement by two newspapers, Vecernji List and Vjesnik. That was in 1997.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: Correct. I think that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: And that after that fact, that information was published by a number of other newspapers, including your newspaper, Slobodna Dalmacija, at that time in 1997?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: And in 1997, Stjepan Mesic had not yet testified in the Blaskic trial. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: No. He hadn't. He testified in 1998, in March.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: Specifically 16 March to 19 March 1998?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: So the oral order that was issued prior to Mesic testifying in 1998, at the time the 1997 witness statement was disseminated, had not been issued, the oral order that allowed or required Mr. Mesic to testify in closed session?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: Well, it could not possibly have been issued because his testimony had not occurred.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we can't examine a witness on something he claims he doesn't know, and he was very clear about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerson, please move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it's not a matter of him not actually knowing; it's just a matter of me asking some follow-up questions so that we are of the same mind. If you would give me some latitude on this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: And I can make a proffer what the relevance is, if you're interested in. A big part of the defence has been that this was public record information, and my point with this line of questioning is that what was disseminated was Mr. Mesic's witness statement, and that was prior to the 1998 oral order to go into closed session. So it's -- they are two different bodies of information. If you allow me to proceed, I'll go very briefly through this line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: I'll ask this question more simply, Mr. Jovic. On March 16th, Judge Jorda -- and you've read the transcripts of Mr. Mesic's testimony, obviously, yes?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: You need to respond verbally to the questions, not just nod. And so you know that Judge Jorda ordered that Mesic testify in closed session on March 16th, 1998. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: So when these two newspapers had disseminated his witness statement in 1997, that closed-session order did not yet exist. You would agree with that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And you're aware that in 1997 even there was an order of a court in response to that dissemination of information by Vecernji List and Vjesnik, are you not? There's an order of this Court, of the Trial Chamber here at the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: Fair enough. I just want to take you back to when you said that in 1997 Mesic himself had admitted that he testified at the Tribunal. This is on page 23, line 21 of the transcript. Do you recall saying that in your testimony?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: I said 1998, after he appeared at this Tribunal. That was when he admitted that he had appeared as a protected witness. He did so on many different occasions, in fact. I quoted the relevant sources where he stated this for the public record.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: Fair enough. I'm going to talk about some of the articles that you had brought before the Tribunal today for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: Could the usher put annex C on the overhead projector, please. This is annex C of Defence counsel's exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: While that exhibit is being placed on the overhead projector, I just have a couple of questions, Mr. Jovic, that we can just get out of the way. Do you recall the circumstances when Mr. Mesic -- strike that. You had referred to Vecernji List and Vjesnik as having received a leak of the witness statement, and thereafter publishing it in their newspapers. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: And of course you recounted that story of that leak in your newspaper a number of times where you allege that the Defence counsel had actually leaked that statement?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: That was our information at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: And even in 1997, as a result of that leak by Defence counsel, Mr. Mesic was confronted publicly with the information of a leak, leaked information. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: I can't comment on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: If you could take a look at what -- at the exhibit that is on the overhead projector to your left, Mr. Jovic. It was -- it is what was marked as annex C, and it purports to be an article from the Feral Tribune on the 23rd of March, 1998. That was presented by your Defence counsel earlier. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: And in this article which is published shortly after Mr. Mesic testifies; correct? Am I right in that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: That's right. It was published several days after his testimony, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: Correct. And in this article, the article does not go into the content of Mr. Mesic's testimony, does it?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: The article here reveals the identity of a protected witness. In fact, it is the witness himself who does that. And that was the primary purpose of protective measures to begin with.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: What Mr. Mesic says in this article is that: "I testified in the process against General Blaskic about the circumstances familiar to me but which I can't explain more," and it says detalija [phoen], I presume that's a translation issue, and the translation is cut off, but I presume that he then explains that he testified in closed session. So Mr. Mesic himself is telling the newspaper --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Prosecutor has no right to twist things around. We do see what it says. The Prosecutor has just stated a fact that is simply not true. He is confusing the witness. Mr. Mesic didn't say anything other than what's stated here and it's crystal clear. He said: "The circumstances that I am familiar with but that I am unable to offer any detailed interpretation of." The translation stops right there. "Because I promised the President of the Chamber that I would not comment on the proceedings." The Prosecutor has no right to twist his words, and his words are right there for all of us to see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What are you saying is correct in what the Prosecutor has said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecutor says the translation stops right there, but then Mr. Mesic goes on to explain why he was a protected witness. In fact, he doesn't, not at all. He's crystal clear on the issue. He says he's not going to comment on that because he so promised the President of the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: I can live with that interpretation, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: The point being, Mr. Jovic, that in this article Mr. Mesic's -- the content of his testimony is not published. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: Correct, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much --

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: But he is crystal clear here when he says it was no sort of secret testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness please be allowed to finish his answer? He was interrupted in mid-stream and I think he should be allowed to finish his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Have you finished?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. President Mesic states in quite definite terms in this very interview that it was no secret testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: Can I have annex D placed on the overhead projector, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: Mr. Jovic, can you familiarise yourself with that document just very briefly. That is what was briefly presented to you as annex D. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: And that is an article from Vecernji List on March 23rd, 1998, days after Mr. Mesic completed his testimony in the Blaskic trial. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: And I have the English translation in front of me, and it's the first page of annex D. You can look at the Croatian version of this, and unfortunately the English translation is cut off at the end, so I can't read to the end of the sentence. But in the English version the sentence that -- the first sentence that's relevant is the question where they say: "Why was your testimony secret?" Do you see that? "Why was your testimony secret?"

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: I do, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: And Mr. Mesic's purported response here is that: "I testified in closed session." You see that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: And later the question is asked: "In Blaskic" -- and I'm reading this verbatim from the English translation. This is not proper English but it is what is presented here in the translation. "In Blaskic trial Hague court is trying to establish whether Croatia did or didn't attack Bosnia." Do you see that sentence?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: So the writer of Vecernji List is asking Mr. Mesic a question about the trial, and his response is: "That was the subject of the trial, and I don't want to comment." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: So he doesn't reveal the content of his closed session testimony in this article, does he?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm not prone to interrupt anybody's cross-examination too often, but I find myself compelled to because, again, the Prosecutor is twisting things around. This is not what it says. The first question: "Why was your testimony secret?" And then Mr. Mesic [as interpreted] provides an answer, a sentence-long answer, and that's not where it ends, where the Prosecutor just suggested. There's a whole argument there and it's crystal clear. The same applies to -- well, yes, the Blaskic trial, and so on and so forth. And then the Prosecutor just cuts the sentence off, but there is an entire sentence there. It has a beginning, it has an end, and then he twists the meaning of the sentence. That's not the point. If you allow me, I will read the sentence. "Why did you testify in secret? "I testified in closed session because my testimony before the investigators of The Hague Tribunal had been politicised." Can we have the whole sentence then, please, if we're quoting already. Maybe the meaning in my language and in your language is not the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerson was just checking whether the accused is following his reading of this article.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Bear in mind, Mr. Krsnik, that you'll have an opportunity to re-examine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Although we have to proceed very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether I got the ultimate answer I was looking for, Mr. Jovic, which is that in this article in which he's asked questions about the content of his testimony, Mr. Mesic does not give it.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: No. He says he's asked: "Was the subject Bosnia and Herzegovina?" And he says: "That was the subject of the trial." I wouldn't comment on this question, but he in fact did. At least one thing he did say for sure is what the trial was about. He did reveal that much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: I think that would be hard to deny when you're talking about the Blaskic trial, that it was about those subject matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: But can I now present the witness with what was annex E, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: Mr. Jovic, do you have in front of you what was previously marked as annex E, which is an article from Vjesnik on March 23rd, 1998?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: And again, it's an article about Mr. Mesic testifying against General Blaskic. And anywhere in this article do you see anything about the content of his testimony?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: No, nothing about the content. But, again, he reveals the fact that he appeared as a protected witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Annex F, please, if you could present that to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: Now, annex F was -- it is an article from a newspaper called Jutarnji List dating April 7th, the year 2000. Do you have that in front of you?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: And that purports to be an interview with the Prosecutor Carla del Ponte, Prosecutor of this -- of the Office of the Prosecutor here at this Tribunal, yes?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: And in this interview, she's asked a number of questions and specifically one question where she -- the question is: "What do you think about this government?" This is according to the English translation that was provided to me this morning. Do you see that question in the version that you have in front of you? "What do you think about this government?"

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: It's quite illegible. The print is too small for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: Well, perhaps I will put to you what the English translation says because this is being put forward by your lawyer and you can confirm whether or not this was contained in the article. The question was: "What do you think about this government?" And the answer here that is attributed to Carla del Ponte is: "I think it's great. Your president," referring to Mr. Mesic, "is" -- and that's my assertion, "is a big friend of our court. He was a very important witness on one of our trials and he knows a lot and he was truly" -- and then it's cut off, so I don't think what the rest of her statement is. Can you confirm that that is contained in that article or not?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's what the headline says. And then it goes on to say: "It was beautiful talking to him." Or: "It was wonderful talking to him."

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: She doesn't mention the Blaskic trial, does she?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: Not explicitly, but from the entire context it transpires that this is the precise trial involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: She doesn't mention the content of Mr. Mesic's testimony in the Blaskic trial, does she?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: It seems not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: So in the four annexes that was presented to this Court by your lawyer this morning, annexes C, D, E, and F, the content of the protected testimony of Mr. Mesic in the Blaskic trial was not published. You agree with that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: We were claiming that it was the identity of the protected witness that was disclosed and indirectly the contents of the testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: And I'm putting to you that regarding the content of his testimony, indirectly or directly, it is not contained in these articles. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: The outline of the testimony is contained there, but I can agree with what you say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I find that difficult to understand, I'm afraid. What do you mean the outline of his testimony is -- or are you just not able to face up to the harsh reality that there's no reference to the testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that only subjects of the testimony were mentioned, not the content itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: Moving on to the next point. You -- on page 30 of your -- of the transcript of your testimony, page 30 of outline 1, you said that in the year 2000 when Mr. Mesic ran for president people wanted to know if he had testified. Do you remember saying that this morning? And we can have your transcript read back to you if you don't recall saying that.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: No, there's no need for that. I attended numerous journalist conferences where precisely that question -- that issue was raised.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: So my question to you is this: If you're saying that when Mesic ran for president in 2000 people wanted to know if he had testified, then the fact of his identity as a protected witness was still unknown to a lot of people. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: Those were leading questions which showed that the people knew of it, rather than they didn't know. Without that sort of information, it wouldn't have been possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: Let me just ask the question a different way. You said that the people wanted to know if he testified, and then you proceeded to run a number of stories that publicised the fact that he was a protected witness and your lawyer described that as good copy for you. So it obviously was a newsworthy issue that he was a witness.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: This was merely seeking the confirmation of what people had already known. They had known that he had been a protected witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to get to your articles in a second, and we'll revisit that point. In the year 2000 you testified here earlier, and it's on page 30 of outline 12, that you received a parcel that contained CD-ROMs. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: Now, the contents of those CD-ROMs are a little bit unclear to me so I'm going to go through these. You said they contained transcripts of testimony. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: Two CDs contained the content of the testimony, I've already said that, and the third CD contained the text published on the official web page of the ICTY.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: It was good you had predicted my next question, because the text of what was published on the ICTY web site that was contained on that CD-ROM is what I want to talk about now. Okay?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: The text that was on the web site as provided in a document by your Defence counsel today is not the closed session testimony of Mr. Mesic in the Blaskic trial, is it?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: It contained the session at which it was decided that the testimony should be carried out in a -- in closed session. So it clearly showed that he was to testify in closed session.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: I'll ask the question again. That CD did not contain the transcripts of Mr. Mesic's closed-session testimony in the Blaskic trial, did it?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: No, not the testimony itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You had said that it was very easy for you to verify or for maybe your investigators to verify or authenticate, I think is the word that you used, based on the web page what was on the CD. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: And specifically what you're referring to is that on the CD where the transcript of the argument that was made by the lawyers that Mr. Mesic should proceed in closed session was easily verifiable because that was on the web page of the ICTY. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: Evidently. Evidently it was to be found there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: Now, these CD-ROMs that you had obtained also contained the actual transcripts of his closed-session testimony. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct. Those were separate CDs. All these contents were not to be found on one CD.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: And you could not verify on the ICTY web site whether these transcripts were accurate because they were not contained -- the transcript of Mr. Mesic's testimony because they were not contained or published on the ICTY web site. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: I think they were published. I think they were taken from the web pages and then saved.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: You stated here that the transcripts of the hearing to go into closed session was on the web page, on the ICTY web page, yes?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The ruling to move to -- into closed session.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: The point I'm making, Mr. Jovic, is that Mr. Mesic's closed-session transcripts of his testimony were not on the ICTY web page?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: Part of the closed session was, a small part of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: What evidence do you have of that, because nothing has been presented to this Court this morning. What evidence do you have that any closed-session transcript was put on an ICTY web page?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: One should look into the transcripts. I can't speak off the cuff. There is the ruling to move into closed session, and I believe that for some time after that there's still text running.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: The question remains: Do you have any evidence whatsoever that the transcript of his testimony was published?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: The transcript of the testimony itself was not published. I never claimed that --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you --

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: -- and I'm referring to the transcript from the Blaskic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: Let's now talk about the publications in Slobodna Dalmacija themselves. I'm going to start with November 27th.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: Do you have the exhibits that could be presented to Mr. Jovic in order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is it best to follow these from the binders or from the supplement you gave us?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: I suppose the binders, Your Honour, would be the easiest so we're all on the same page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: I would like to present first what's been marked as Prosecution -- what has been admitted into evidence as Prosecution Exhibit 11, tab 1, which is the November 27th issue of Slobodna Dalmacija.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: Do you have that exhibit in front of you, tab 1, Exhibit 11, Mr. Jovic? It's your newspaper from November 27th. Do you have that issue in front of you, Mr. Jovic?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: And were you the editor-in-chief on this day that this was published?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: On the cover you -- one of the headlines, and this is page 1 of the English translation, it's stated that: "This is the first full and accurate testimony by Stjepan Mesic at The Hague Tribunal on 19 April 1997." Do you see that headline on the front of your paper?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: To be quite honest, this is not his testimony; it's actually his witness statement, to be precise, that's published in this newspaper. Yes?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: This must have been a mistake, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: Let's go to the second page of the November 27th issue. And you'll see another headline at the very top -- it's actually page 7 of November 27th. Do you have page 7 in front of you?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I mistakenly referred to it as the second page, but it's the seventh page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: Because it refers the same mistake you refer to on the cover is made on page 7, where it says: "The transcript from The Hague, the complete testimony of Stjepan Mesic before The Hague court on 19 April 1997."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I should allow Mr. Jovic to answer. He already spotted what this is about.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This text above the headline obviously contains an error. It says here: "In four instalments we will be publishing the contents of the first testimony," and this is precisely what you've been talking about. It says here that he testified before the Tribunal twice, which is also imprecision.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: Mr. Jovic, when you say "it says here," we need to be precise for the record. On page 7, in the bottom right-hand corner, there's a darkened box. And it starts with "Stjepan Mesic." Is that what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: This is page --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The same box, but that's the second bullet or item.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: In the English translation it's page 2 of 7, and at the very bottom of the page and it's titled "inset."

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: And here very clearly -- and it says at the bottom that it's written by the editor. And that is you, is it not?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: No. It says that it was the team of investigators of Slobodna Dalmacija who authored this. I myself didn't edit the text in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: Referring to the inset box that's darkened, can you read the last line of that inset box? It's a line that concludes with the word "editor."

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: I don't see that. I see that it says the headings are produced by the board of editors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, again it's either an error in interpretation, but in the original it says that the headings are those of the board of editors. The editor himself is not mentioned anywhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The board of editors. You'll accept that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: I'll accept that, yes, the board of editors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: And are you -- at that time, were you on the board of editors as the editor-in-chief, Mr. Jovic?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: I answered that. The editor-in-chief, of course, is the head of the board of editors.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And in this inset box, Mr. Jovic, you very clearly set out the difference between Mr. Mesic's witness statement that he gave to the Tribunal on April 19th and his testimony in the Blaskic trial, which you or the board of editors state, quite clearly, was a confidential one, do you not?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: It is stated that it was confidential.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: Let's go to the next exhibit -- the next tab in Exhibit 11, which is tab 2, and this is November 28th, the year 2000. And actually direct your attention to page 7, again.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, while this is getting set up, this would be page 2 of the English translation. And again, there's an inset box in the translation that begins with: "On his own initiative ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: Mr. Jovic, do you have page 7 in front of you of your November 28th issue?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have it before me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: And again, the very top of the page repeats the error from the first issue, which is: "The complete testimony of Stjepan Mesic before The Hague Tribunal on the 19th of April" is repeated, is it not?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: Evidently. But the editors were obviously unaware of the circumstances in which his first testimony was given.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Jovic, as the editor of this paper, aren't you interested in making sure that what is published in the paper is as accurate as possible?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: There's another inset box at the bottom of this page that I'd like to refer you to. Do you see that? It's slightly darkened.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
