utterances.text: It is basically a repeat from the previous day, but the language is slightly modified, because this time it says: "Mesic's second testimony was secret, at his own request." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: Now, of course you've got the -- you received this information on a CD-ROM that contained the full arguments by Blaskic's Defence counsel and the OTP Prosecutors --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Apologies. I must intervene because the Prosecutor is misinterpreting the evidence again. The two texts are absolutely identical in the original. Both the text published on the 27th and the one on the 28th of November are quite identical. There's not a single difference, and I can't see why the Prosecutor is saying that they're slightly different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: I think that's correct. I think they are identical. I just got different translations for the same Croatian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: Mr. Jovic, let me ask you this then because I have two different English translations, one which says that -- the translation was: "Mesic testified confidentially," and this one says that he testified "secretly" or "was secret." Are both of those accurate translations or which one is more accurate in your mind?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: Both terms may be treated as synonymous in the Croatian language.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: Fair enough. I'm going to move on now to December 3rd. You do, in fact, publish two more instalments of Mesic's witness statement on the 30th -- on the 29th and the 30th, correct, but we don't go into them here because they're largely the same. Yes, do you agree?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: You receive -- the next day you receive a cease and desist order from a Trial Chamber I in the Blaskic case, via facsimile is what you testified, yes?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: And that cease and desist order is published in its entirety, word for word, on December 3rd. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: As well as on the front page of December 3rd you feature the fact that you received a cease and desist order, do you not?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I think we should present the witness with what is tab 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: Do you have the December 3rd edition in Croatian in front of you?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: I'm going to read for you my English translation of one of the major headlines on this edition, and you can tell me whether this translation is accurate. It says: "The Hague Tribunal has forbidden Slobodna Dalmacija further publishing of Mesic's testimony." Is that an accurate translation?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: So that would suggest to me, Mr. Jovic, that you had a pretty clear understanding of the cease and desist order?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: I've spoken about that already. At the time I had received assurances and I believed that this order was not directly in relation to me as a citizen of the Republic of Croatia. I believed that this order could only be enforced through the Croatian judiciary.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: This cease and desist order is directed at Slobodna Dalmacija, by name, is it not?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: But similar orders were sent to the Croatian judiciary, weren't they? I was expecting a certain procedure in that sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: I'm going to get to that in a moment, the different legal opinions that you sought. But my question right now is that: This cease and desist order was served on Slobodna Dalmacija by name, of which you were the editor-in-chief, right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: It was faxed through to Slobodna Dalmacija, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: And at the bottom of that order, if you received, admittedly received, it says that Slobodna Dalmacija must stop publishing the statements and the transcripts of testimony of the protected witness, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But again, my understanding was not that we had to implement that order directly without appropriate decisions from the Croatian judiciary and its bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: So what you're telling this Chamber is that there was something ambiguous about that order in your mind?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. I did not mean to knowingly violate that order, as you claim. I was waiting. I may have erred, but I was waiting for a certain procedure within Croatia to kick in. But then I also received the interpretations that I have already elaborated on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: So I want to ask you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What procedure were you waiting on to kick in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Constitutional law of Croatia says that the cooperation of Croatia and Croatian citizens with the ICTY can only go through the government office for cooperation. There is no direct contact, in other words. I was expecting an order like that, one similar to the one that you sent to Croatia and Slobodna Dalmacija, to reach me from a body belonging to the Croatian judiciary pursuant to your own order. For example, I was arrested pursuant to a decision of a Croatian court, but that decision itself was pursuant to a ruling of The Hague court, which means that I was not arrested and kept in detention for a week pursuant to an order from The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: Mr. Jovic, you state here that this cease and desist order that was faxed to your office that you received, that says to stop publishing statements and testimony of Mesic, was ambiguous to you. So my question -- and you sought different legal opinions. But you went ahead and published anyways, didn't you? And you put on the front page of your paper that you were publishing in contravention of the cease and desist order, do you not?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: I stopped publishing until I received the appropriate explanations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: What additional explanations did you seek from Trial Chamber I in the Blaskic Trial Chamber that had issued the decision? If you were so concerned about the ambiguity of their cease and desist order, what additional clarity did you seek from Trial Chamber I?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: I have told you already who it was that I was expecting an explanation from, and it wasn't the Trial Chamber. Maybe it's an omission on my part. But I thought that this was down to the government office for cooperation, to seek that sort of explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: So you made no attempts to seek any clarification from Trial Chamber I?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: Not directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: So you deliberate on the front pages of your paper on December 3rd, 4th, and 5th. Let's go now to December 6th.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: And if you can present the witness tab 8 of Exhibit 11, the December 6th edition of Slobodna Dalmacija.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: Do you have that edition in front of you, Mr. Jovic?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: What is the major headline of the December 6th edition?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: "Slobodna reveals a Hague secret."

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: Now, if you're -- the legal opinions that you obtained that gave you a contrary interpretation of the cease and desist order served directly on you, this is not true because you didn't consider it a secret at all, did you?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the headline itself was phrased to attract readers. That's how it goes. A certain amount of poetic license is always involved in phrasing headlines.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: And perhaps a certain amount of license would allow you to come up with your own interpretation of a cease and desist order so that you could publish transcripts, which also sells papers, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: I don't agree. That certainly wasn't my motive.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: If I could turn your attention to page 3 of the December 6th issue ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: If I could refer Your Honours' attention to page 6 of the English transcript of this tab.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: Mr. Jovic, I want to read to you the English translation that I have from the -- it's a blocked box on the right-hand side of that page, page 3, right in the middle, two columns, a block of text. And it says -- my English translation is the following. "Despite this fact and despite the order from the Tribunal in The Hague, which threatens Slobodna Dalmacija with penalties which we also made public, we decided, notwithstanding the risk, to publish instalments of the whole contents of Mesic's mysterious testimony given before the Tribunal on March 16th to 19th." Is that a fair translation of the Croatian version?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But I wrote "mysterious," and there's a certain amount of irony involved, you know. It means that it was and wasn't secret at the same time, if you see what I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: Well, that interpretation contradicts the headlines on the paper, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: The headline of your paper says "secret testimony, secret revealed," doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: So what seems to be in contradiction to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: I'll move on. Never mind. There's also an article which is page 6 of the English translation. And my English translation of this article is -- of this Croatian version is: "Six reasons why Slobodna is publishing Mesic's testimony." Do you see that article, Mr. Jovic?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: In the middle of the page, on page 6 of the English translation there's a sentence that starts with: "Firstly," which is the first reason that Slobodna Dalmacija gives. I want you to confirm whether or not this is an accurate translation of the Croatian. It says: "Stjepan Mesic is no longer under any danger because there's no longer Tudjman or his media or secret services, which were the reasons why he felt he should be protected." Is that a fair translation?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: The second provision here that -- the second reason that you give that you're violating the court order is that the body of editors has decided to publish his testimony out of public interest. I'm paraphrasing because it's a longer paragraph. But you're --

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: That's the third reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: Well, it starts with the phrase "secondly." The third reason is very similar, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: But it's not what you suggest, public interest, that's not in connection with the second reason. It's in connection with the third reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: Fair enough. Let me read the second reason then and there won't be any dispute. The second reason that you give is: "Mesic is presently the president of Croatia and no longer an ordinary citizen, and if he doesn't feel the need to reveal what he discussed" --

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: That you're going to do it for him is what you say. If he doesn't feel the need to do it, you're going to do it for him, in contravention of the court order. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: There is no contravention of a court order there, if you are quoting me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: The third reason that you give is that there's a big and reasonable interest of the public for publication of the contents of the testimony.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: Of the present head of state.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: The fourth reason you give is that Mesic alone was the initiator of the practice of the publication of secret documents. Now, my question there is that by your own admission the first leak of information was by the Defence counsel in the Blaskic case, so this would be an inaccurate statement, would it not?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: This statement is in relation to secret documents that not only have to do with the ICTY but also with the transcripts from President Tudjman's office that he distributed to journalists, and those were classified documents. It's a matter of violation of a more general principle.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: The fifth represent that you give is that the Tribunal in The Hague has no competences over citizens of the Republic of Croatia. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: That's right. That's what it says. Nevertheless, this calls for an explanation, and it's an explanation that I've already provided. There is no direct competence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: Mr. Jovic, if you've already provided an explanation, there's no reason to provide a second one. Let me just move quickly on to the sixth reason you give, which is that you're publishing Mesic's secret testimony because one of those entrusted with the confidentiality was Blaskic's Defence lawyer, Anto Nobilo, who distributed the disk containing Mesic's testimony. Yes, is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: None of these reasons comport with your explanation to the Court today that you sought out a number of legal opinions that said the material wasn't protected. So how do you explain that difference to this Chamber today?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: There is nothing contradictory there, nothing mutually exclusive. I'm talking about the reason I'm interested in these documents. What I said before was about the logic of law and about legal procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: Mr. Jovic, without going into the rest of the issues of Slobodna Dalmacija, this is December 6th. You publish more of Mesic's closed-session testimony on December 7th, do you not?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: And on December 8th?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: We later continued.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: And you do the same on December 8th?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: Let's put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: Up until December 29th. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: And on each of these articles you indicate that this is the secret testimony of a protected witness, Stjepan Mesic, in the Blaskic trial, do you not?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was declared to be a secret, as I said. However, a lot had already been disclosed by this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: And in those 22 editions you published every single word of the transcript of Stjepan Mesic in his closed-session testimony before this Tribunal, did you not?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: We published what we had. I'm not sure that that was all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: I want to ask you one final question, Mr. Jovic, and it's a statement that you made on page 57 of your transcript, about line 1. You said something to the effect, and I'm paraphrasing because I don't have it in front of me, but you didn't know that you were publishing something, you thought you were allowed to publish it. Do you remember making that statement? You didn't know that you were publishing something that was protected, that you were allowed to publish. And if you don't recall, I can have that statement -- your statement read to you.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: I no longer remember myself what exactly it was that I said. However, what I meant was -- I was believing that I was publishing something that I had every right to publish and something that I was never banned from publishing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: And if you thought you had the right to publish this and that it was not, in fact, protected, that would not allow you to state in a dramatic brazen way, each and every day for 22 straight days, that this was secret, protected material that would allow you to sell newspapers, would it?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: That's just a headline. It was automatically generated from one issue to the next. It wasn't our intention to taunt, if that's what you mean. As I said, it was a secret but a secret that had, to a large extent, already been revealed. And by whom? By the very people involved in the trial, all of them, in fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerson, we are up against time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: I know. One last question, Your Honours, and it's very brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: One of the opinions that you sought was Mr. Josipovic, Professor Josipovic, that you're -- right, is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: This is tab 8 of Exhibit 11. And I'll refer to the Court page 1 of 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: Do you have that exhibit in front of you, Mr. Jovic?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: And you state that one of the sources that you relied on for your legal advice and consultation was Professor Josipovic, yes?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: I just want to direct your attention to a clause. It's the bottom of the page 1 of 6, and this is your -- the advice that you're getting that you're relying on to come up with a different interpretation than the cease and desist order. And I'm going to read you the English translation. The sentence goes: "The Tribunal could change its decision, should it realise that the reasons for which it declared some documents confidential no longer exist." Do you see that sentence?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: It says -- the counsel that you got was and that you published in your newspaper was that the Tribunal could change its decision. That would suggest to me that you were obligated, if one wants to believe that you had the right to seek alternative legal opinion, but your own counsel is suggesting that you should apply to this Tribunal for a modification of the cease and desist order, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, again it's a mistranslation, but this needs to be taken up with Mr. Jovic because the meaning here is totally different. I think this needs to be clarified because what the Prosecutor is saying is not accurate.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, this is more a comment on what Mr. Josipovic originally said. Mr. Josipovic is obviously quite reserved, himself, on this issue, as far as the formal and legal jurisdiction of the court is concerned in this instance. Aside from that, he's not our counsel officially. He's not here in an official capacity. And then in this same piece we have opinions that are totally different. Zdravko Tomac, take one example, he was the vice-president of the Croatian parliament. There's another politician from another party who is also a foremost legal expert in Croatia, Josko Moric. That's just an opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: The question I have for you: Is it an accurate translation, first and foremost, because I can't read Croatian. But the English says: "The Tribunal could change its decision, should it realise the reasons for confidentiality no longer exist." "The Tribunal could change its decision," is that what it says there?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think that's what it says verbatim. I says --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Mr. Ackerson, could you pay attention what is stated in page 12 of 12. Is it the identical passage? Why don't you give it a try to put it to the witness. Here it says: "The Tribunal should change its decision." It's slightly different.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: Mr. Jovic I'm going to read to you a passage, it's going to take me a moment to find where the Croatian version of this is, though. This must be an insert box which is at the end of an article which is entitled -- it's written by Ante -- I'm going to massacre this name, but Zuzo or Gujo. And the article is entitled: "The President needs the international tribunal" -- There's an insert box at the end of that article, and I'm going to put this to you for your comment, Mr. Jovic. "This is the first case" -- and tell me if you see this insert box. "This is the first case in which the International Criminal Tribunal addresses the media through a separate order in any state. If viewed from a formal and legal point of view this Tribunal has the competence for such conduct. However, every decision delivered by the Tribunal, including this one, is a subject of criticism and further investigation. The Tribunal should change its decision in the case of expiry of reasons why some materials have been declared confidential." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: "The Tribunal should change its decision."

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps you could finish reading that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: "They should do the same in the case if there no longer exist security reasons which would be preponderant in relation to the obvious interests of the public to find out a certain detail from the hearing, said Professor Josipovic." "They" in this case being the Tribunal, no?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: What it should do, that's in reference to the Court, isn't it, that the Court should do this. That's his suggestion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: The point being: He's not saying that you should do this; he's saying that the Court is obligated to make this change, isn't he? I need --

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what he says.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik, briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Jovic, I was under the impression that we had sufficiently clarified matters, but upon hearing the cross-examination and the questions by Judges I want to clarify the following. What were you waiting for from the Croatian authorities? Were you waiting for an order to be issued on the part of the Croatian judiciary or were you waiting for something else? Please tell us, were you waiting for a ruling by the judiciary?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's precisely what I was waiting for.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Why don't you tell us this?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: I believed that I had stated this clearly enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Well, that's not the case.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: I was expecting some sort of a position, a ruling, or any sort of opinion by some official authority of the Republic of Croatia --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, aside from the fact that it's probably beyond the scope of my examination, it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't think it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: -- been asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It may have been leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: That's the third and final -- it's extraordinarily leading and that would be my own --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Don't lead -- I suggest you go ahead, proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I don't know if this is a leading question if I say: Were you expecting the Croatian court to pass down a ruling banning you from publishing the documents any further? Is this a leading question? Were you expecting this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's leading. That's leading. You would have to ask him what he was expecting or tell him what he should expect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Mr. Jovic, I will not put any further questions to you, but you can see that this matter has not been clarified. What were your expectations, what did you expect, and what were to be your follow-up steps? And please focus. I think this is the core of misunderstanding here.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that the Croatian authorities had received the same or a similar order from the ICTY, I was waiting for their reaction, namely an order or a ruling banning any further publication of the transcripts. Since I received no such rulings, I sought suggestions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Could you please be more precise. What sort of suggestions or opinions were you seeking?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: I wanted to obtain an opinion that I was not breaking the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Who were you asking these opinions from?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: From the public prosecutor's office in the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Had you received any such order from a Croatian court?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: I would have complied with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: An order from whom?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: From the public prosecutor's office or a court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Which court? Could you please be specific?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: From the -- from a court of the Republic of Croatia, be it municipal or county court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: You mentioned your arrest and detention. Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: I was arrested pursuant to a ruling by the county court of Split, which followed after the ICTY had issued an -- a warrant for arrest --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I fully respect any instructions from you. I am not versed in common-law procedure, and I'm trying to explain my case on the basis of mens rea, because as you were able to see the witness is answering my questions sincerely, but we have to clarify matters. Was he -- did he know or didn't he know, because do you really believe that people in Croatia understand the meaning of an order or the difference between an out-of-court and in-court testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Mr. Jovic, do you have any legal experience? Are you a lawyer?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the law system in the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: Just as any other ordinary citizens would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Do you know the procedure before the Tribunals? Do you know that there's a difference between the investigating procedure and trial?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I still have questions of the witness, Your Honours, we still have to clarify certain matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: My idea is that we have to finish today and in ten, 15 minutes. So I'm going to allow five minutes for closing addresses. Issues are fairly clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the matters are clear enough, I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, I just want to make sure, have you finished your re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Your Honour stated that the matters are clear, and I decided that there was no need for me to further re-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll have seven minutes each for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Before the closing addresses, I have to say that the Chamber will admit the five exhibits that the Defence has sought to produce. We will not allow the additional two witnesses. They are both to deal with issues of mens rea, and the Chamber considers that it has heard enough evidence in relation to that issue. For the closing addresses, seven minutes each. Mr. -- Who is to begin? Mr. Ackerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Perhaps the most important, pivotal bit of evidence that you heard occurred just five minutes ago, and it was at line 108 -- I'm sorry, page 108, line 16 of your transcript, and Mr. Jovic says in response to a question: What kind of legal opinions were you seeking after he got the cease and desist order? And his answer was: "I wanted to obtain an opinion that I was not breaking the law." Now, he receives a cease and desist order on December 1st, which is crystal clear. It's served on his newspaper. He's the editor-in-chief, he fully acknowledges that he receives it. He publishes it in his paper. He proceeds to issue 22 -- 25 issues of his newspaper that clearly indicate that he knows exactly what this order is telling him that he can't do and that he's intentionally and brazenly violated. Now, his reason, or his defence today is that he obtained other legal opinions and that those other legal opinions, according to him, allowed him -- differed from the cease and desist order interpretation, that the material wasn't protected. And so there's a number of responses to that. First of all, one of those legal opinions clearly didn't say that; Mr. Josipovic. Secondly, if you, as a Chamber, allow third parties, such as newspapers, to second-guess an order of a Trial Chamber, I would submit you're opening a door to watering down your ability to control these proceedings. We ask witnesses to come here and testify under life-threatening conditions. And they do so because we assure them that we can guarantee their confidentiality when we testify in closed session. And that's a decision that you, as Judges, have to make after hearing the arguments of the parties. And those decisions are not going to be perfect, but those decisions have to be respected. They have to be sacrosanct. And if you deviate from that policy, we cannot rightfully ask witnesses to come in and look them in the eye and tell them that our guarantees of confidentiality, even when ordered by a Court, will be backed up by this Tribunal. So we're asking you to back up your own word -- this was the Blaskic Trial Chamber that heard the arguments of the parties, and that's an exhibit in the binder, and the arguments of the parties laid out the fact that Mr. Mesic, President Mesic -- the Defence counsel in the Blaskic case had leaked his witness statement and that that had been publicised by the newspapers. That was taken into account by the Blaskic Trial Chamber. And they heard parties from -- they heard arguments from Defence counsel on the issue, they heard the arguments of the Prosecution, and they decided to allow President Mesic to testify in closed session. That order has to be backed up by this Trial Chamber. What Slobodna Dalmacija did was intentionally and repeatedly violate this court order, and why they did it doesn't really matter. Whether they were trying to sell newspapers, whether they were politically motivated, the simple case is that this is not a case about damage to President Mesic; this is a case about violating a court order. And as this Chamber decided in the Bulatovic decision in Milosevic, that a knowing and wilful interference with the administration of justice necessarily follows when someone defies a court order, and you have no clearer example of a defiance of a court order than you have right now, and you cannot allow a third party such as a newspaper to forum shop for a different legal opinion to avoid the force and effect of a Court order, because I can tell you that, you know, by way of metaphor, if someone is charged with possession of cocaine in a country, there will be lots of people who will say that drug laws are invalid and improper and, in their opinion, they should not be respected. It's the law and the Court's order that matters, and ignorance of the law is not a defence. I will say one other comment because it has been raised by this Chamber about the delay in the prosecution. This occurred in 2000. The indictment was brought in 2005, and I would just direct the Court's attention that when this occurred, in the 29 issues where Slobodna Dalmacija, and specifically 25 issues where they were repeatedly and directly violating a cease and desist order, the Prosecution issued four notices to the Blaskic Trial Chamber, indicating that there were repeated violations of the cease and desist order. On January 26th, 2001, the Blaskic Trial Chamber issued a decision that said two things: One, that it was directing the Registry to conduct an investigation. In essence, they were conducting their own investigation, but it was the Registry that was going to be doing it for the Chambers; and they said they remained seized of the matter, that they noted that the Prosecution had made four notices of these violations, and they remained seized of the matter. And they proceeded to remain seized of the matter until May of 2005, when they finally directed the Prosecution to conduct its own investigation. And at that point, six weeks later, we filed the indictment against Mr. Jovic. So the matter was not in the hands of the Prosecution during that time. We filed proper notice when the violations were occurring, and we took six weeks to file an indictment once we were given the authority to do so. Thank you very much. I appreciate the opportunity --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerson, I only regret not having enough time on this, but I wonder if you have anything to comment upon the issues raised by the Defence which is related to freedom of media or right of the public to know. And this is related to the -- to a president of a republic and apparently there seems to be no more reasons for protective measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: The first response that I would make to that argument -- because that is I think superficially an interesting argument, but if you explore it I don't think it is -- it has much merit. What you do in the serious cases that you try involves high-ranking political figures and high-ranking military figures, and they often are going to be given protections, either in the form of pseudonyms or closed-session orders, despite the fact that they are public figures because they are willing to come forward on those guarantees. The important thing in this case that Mesic was a well-known figure in Croatia, and that was part of the arguments that was put forward very clearly by Blaskic's Defence counsel that Mesic should not be allowed to testify in closed session. Once the Court decided that he should testify in closed session, the issue is no longer a free-speech issue, it is merely an issue of whether or not a third party can interpret a Court's order and in its own mind determine that it has been lifted. What the Defence is asking you to do is to say that once somebody violates the closed-session order, it's now public domain, and therefore a criminal act or a contemptuous act is the same as a court order lifting that protection, and that will have disastrous consequences for us. Because the reality is that there are leaks. There are unintentional leaks sometimes here, and if you equate a court order with those actions, we have very little ability to protect our witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I haven't heard such hypocritical comments as put forward by my learned friend from the Prosecution for a long time, especially in response to Judge, His Honour, Kwon's question. Well, suffice it to say that back in 1998 Mr. Mesic was not a president and that he was accorded protective measures. It was in January of 2000 that he was elected president and then enjoyed all the protection that a president enjoys. But before that period, there weren't such reasons in place. Your Honours, we are a small people, but nevertheless we watch closely what is going on. The only thing that someone had to do from the ICTY was to phone President Mesic and ask him whether these protective measures were still necessary or not, because we need to have transparency in our country. Gentlemen, when are we going to make trial records public? In 100 years. If we listen to what the Prosecutor is saying, this will never become open. Is that really the purpose of this institution? I don't wish to respond to such arguments at all. The Prosecution is manipulating the Trial Chamber. It is looking for a precedent, and it wants you to send the following message to the Balkans: Journalists over there, we will not inform you of anything because we have witnesses coming here blackmailing us and telling us that they will not testify unless it's in closed session. But that is not the point of trials. Why don't we put the question to the Prosecution? Why didn't the Prosecution phone President Mesic and ask him whether the protection accorded to him was still necessary and what was the -- what were the measures to protect him from? Don't forget that President Bush came to testify in front of the international court of -- imagine what would happen if he came to testify here before the International Court of Justice in The Hague? We are advocating the principle of equality before the law, but I'm afraid that not all of us are equal before the law, especially in some countries that are not stable democracies. My government did not react when this order was issued. The government should have said: Stop, we have the constitutional law in place, and Mr. Granic and the government stated that. You cannot issue orders to citizens. Let us debate this issue before a court of law, as was, in fact, the case when the Ministry of Defence was issued with a subpoena. And then it was the Appeals Chamber that came to the conclusion that the minister could not be asked to testify. The same should have been done in this case. The government should have looked into the matter, and I'm sure that the journalists, together with Mr. Jovic, would have waited for the outcome of that debate, as he did in fact wait for six days. Mr. Ackerson said that this was quite clear, but I'm sure that nobody in Croatia finds this to be clear, especially not a journalist. That is why he was waiting for a court of law in his own country to tell him what he was supposed to do. The government should have reacted, because under international law, if its own citizen is charged with a criminal conduct, it has to be -- his extradition has to be decided upon. The same is true in this case where the freedom of the media was involved. Nobody could have incurred any consequences as a result of that. The Prosecutor said that a closed session a sacrosanct, but that's not true and cannot be true. Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Why, Mr. Krsnik -- something's just not clear to me. After seeking the advice of the public prosecutor's office, or waiting, as you said, on some kind of a decision from the courts, why did he nonetheless accompany the publication with a statement that he knew the publication was in violation of a -- of the order of the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the matter is quite simple, and I will try to fully explain it. The government, the Ministry of Justice, charged the prosecutor's office of the Republic of Croatia to give their legal opinion whether Mr. Jovic had been breaking the law or not. The Ministry of Justice of the Republic of Croatia had sought this sort of advice from the Croatian public prosecutor's office. The Croatian public prosecutor's office responded by saying that he had not been breaking any laws, especially not those of Croatia, and that he could carry on publishing the documents. The government did the same. They sought the opinion of the public prosecutor's office. The government and the public prosecutor's office -- or rather, the government entrusted the public prosecutor's office to examine whether he was in breach of the law, be it international or domestic. And the public prosecutor's office response was that he was in breach of no law, be it international or domestic. That was why we were referring to the document, the written opinion, that was made and which you should seek through a subpoena. As a result of the information he was given, what sort of a conclusion could he arrive -- have arrived at but to continue publishing? Mr. Jovic testified truthfully before the Chamber. The only thing that remained for him was to make sure his paper was being sold, and of course resorting to the poetic license. But he had not been given a single indication, nor have I heard anything from the Prosecutor today, to show that he should have had a different understanding of the matter. You were able to hear what Mr. Jovic's reasoning was. What we were hearing from the other side was simply matters from the realm of conjecture and surmise, far from evidence. I have to say that Mr. Mesic was not afraid, Mr. Mesic is not a coward. Mr. Mesic always publicly spoke his mind. He was always a courageous politician even at the time of Yugoslavia. When he came into conflict with Tudjman, he always adhered to his principles and he always spoke publicly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We have to vacate this courtroom in two minutes. The tape runs out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, do not render a decision in favour of this indictment because you will deprive every single journalist in the world to follow these trials. Because the journalist is not to blame; the one who is to blame is the one who disclosed this information from the courtroom. Besides, there were other papers and other journalists who published the same information and who were not indicted, and that's hypocritical. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Jovic, are you still the editor-in-chief of the newspaper?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not for the last four years. Not since 2001. I'm now a commentator.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, excuse me, I forgot about the disposition. Can I come on my own for this to be disclosed without Mr. Jovic so that when the judgement is rendered ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll decide that and let you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I know we need to get out of here, but I just think for the record that I need to say something regarding aggravating and mitigating factors, otherwise it's going to be conspicuously absent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERSON
utterances.text: Fair enough. I'll submit that in writing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. We thank the parties for the submissions, and we'll consider the matter and give our decision shortly.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.01 p.m.
